SDM Xtended Table offers extensive customization options organized into logical sections in the Format panel. This guide walks you through each feature section, explaining what it does and where to learn more.

What it controls: The fundamental data display and aggregation settings This section determines: Table type (Percentage vs Mean) Which metrics to display (values, percentages, indices) Data masking patterns Key decisions here: Choose between percentage analysis or mean analysis Toggle vertical/horizontal percentages Enable indice calculations Set up masking patterns for sensitive data When to use: Configure this section first, as it defines what your table displays and how data is aggregated. 📖 Learn more: Table Contents Reference

What it controls: How rows and columns are arranged in your table This section allows you to: Sort rows alphabetically or by column values Specify sorting direction (ascending/descending) Pin specific rows/columns to first or last positions Choose which metric to sort by (value, percentage, indice) Key decisions here: Alphabetical sorting for consistency Value-based sorting for insights (highest sales first) Fixed positioning for totals and special categories When to use: After your data is displaying correctly, configure sorting to highlight insights or maintain consistent presentation. 📖 Learn more: Sorting & Ordering Reference

What it controls: Visual highlighting of top/bottom performers This composite section includes: Basic Settings: Ranking scope, order, and display method Custom Colors: Define your own color gradients Exclude Range: Prevent middle values from being colored Key decisions here: Choose ranking scope (global, per row, per column) Select display format (numbered badges or color gradients) Configure color intensity and schemes When to use: Add ranking after basic table setup to visually emphasize performance differences. 📖 Learn more: Ranking & Visualization Reference

What it controls: Conditional decoration of individual cells (color, label, badge, or full CSS) driven by rules you write directly in the visual This section allows you to: Write condition : output rules, evaluated top-to-bottom on each cell — the first matching rule wins React to the cell's own computed values (pctV, pctH, indice, value, base, avg, signif1, signif2) and to header labels (colN, rowN for any level N) Color backgrounds or text, prepend labels, add colored badges, or apply full custom CSS (gradients, bold, alignment…) Add a default catch-all for cells no other rule matches Key decisions here: Choose the display mode (cell background, text color, label, badge, or Custom CSS) Write conditions with numeric and header variables (remember pctV/pctH are fractions 0–1) Pick a badge shape when using badge mode When to use: When you need conditional formatting that reacts to the numbers the visual actually displays — no DAX measure required. 📖 Learn more: Cell Rules Reference

What it controls: Data series mapping for percentage tables This section appears when Table Type is set to "Percentage" and manages: Value series (the counts to display) Base series (denominators for percentages) Unweighted base series Significance testing series Effective base series Key decisions here: Map your data measures to appropriate series Configure weighted vs unweighted bases Set up series for statistical testing When to use: Essential for percentage tables with custom measures or weighted data. info There is no Multiple answer toggle here: how group bases are built is now a per-level property, Sample across items. See Sample Across Items. 📖 Learn more: Percentage Series Configuration

What it controls: Data series mapping for mean tables This section appears when Table Type is set to "Mean" and manages: Mean series (the averages to display) Count series (sample sizes) Standard deviation series Significance testing series for means Unweighted base series Key decisions here: Map your numerical measures Include sample size information Configure standard deviation for statistical analysis When to use: Essential for mean tables to properly aggregate and display average values. 📖 Learn more: Mean Series Configuration

What it controls: Statistical testing and difference highlighting This composite section includes: Base Settings: Test types, confidence levels, variance methods Test 1 Configuration: Display and comparison options Test 2 Configuration: Additional test layer Key decisions here: Choose test type (all columns, item vs total, regex) Set confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%) Select visual display method (icon, color, border) When to use: When you need to highlight statistically significant differences between groups. 📖 Learn more: Significance Testing Reference

What it controls: Display of total rows, base rows, and subtotals This section manages: Total column display Base row configuration Unweighted base row Subtotals for hierarchical levels (chosen per column level from the Column Headers editor) Base row positioning (top/bottom) Custom labels for special rows Key decisions here: Show/hide totals and bases Position base rows at top or bottom Customize row labels Configure subtotals for multi-level tables — on by default at every level When to use: Configure after basic table setup to add context rows. 📖 Learn more: Totals & Subtotals Reference

What it controls: Data quality warnings and value masking This section allows you to: Set warning thresholds (visual alerts) Set masking thresholds (hide values) Choose threshold basis (cell value, base, unweighted base) Configure empty cell display for zero values Key decisions here: Warning level for small sample sizes Masking level for data protection What to base thresholds on When to use: Important for survey data or any analysis with variable sample sizes. 📖 Learn more: Thresholds & Masking Reference
What it controls: Visual appearance and styling This composite section includes multiple cards:
Hover highlighting Zebra rows Selection mode Percentage symbol display Decimal precision Freeze panes and forbid horizontal scroll Row title width Column header visibility Transparent background
Pre-defined style themes (Custom, Modern, Classic, Scientific, Market Research) Cell text size Color themes (20+ options) Row title text alignment

Cell Format: Data cell appearance Tile Mode: Cells rendered as separated tiles Key decisions here: Choose a theme or create custom styling Set freeze panes for navigation Configure fonts and colors for branding Adjust decimal precision for your audience When to use: Configure styling after data and structure are finalized, or apply pre-defined themes immediately for quick professional appearance. 📖 Learn more: Formatting & Styling Reference

What it controls: The presentation of column and row headers, level by level This card replaces the Top level / Sub level / Row header format cards and the Logo Lv1–Lv3 / Row Logo Lv1–Lv2 roles of CrossTable. It contains two ⚙ editors, Column Headers and Row Headers, plus the Header Logos lookup. For each level, with no ceiling on the number of levels, you can set: Font, color and background Whether the level is shown, and whether it gets a sub-total (columns) The Logo series (an Additional Series measure returning a base64 image) and the logo mode and size For rows: side column or full-width band, and an additional CSS field The size of the data columns and rows (auto, equal, minimal or fixed), the gap before each group, and how long column titles are cut Key decisions here: Provide logos through a measure (Logo series) or, when they only depend on the label, through the Header Logos lookup (no query cost) Decide for each row level between a side column and a full-width band When to use: To style and brand the hierarchy once data and structure are finalized. 📖 Learn more: Table Headers Reference · Logos in Headers · Tutorial: Header Logos

What it controls: How the base of a group (total, sub-total, comparison complement) is built from the items it contains It is a property of each header level, set from the ⚙ editors: Disjoint (the items are different people, bases add up), Shared (the items are answered by the same sample, bases do not add up) or Native (the sub-total is read from your own DAX measure). 📖 Learn more: Sample Across Items
Here's a recommended order for configuring your table:

Table Contents: Choose table type, select what to display Series Configuration: Map your data (% or Mean series) Totals: Add base rows and total columns Sample across items: Declare, per level, whether items share the same sample
Sorting: Arrange for insights or consistency Significance: Highlight statistical differences Ranking: Visual performance indicators Thresholds: Data quality controls
Table Headers: Format each header level, add logos Table Format: Apply styling and themes Fine-tune: Adjust fonts, colors, precision

Some features depend on others: Feature Requires Vertical % Base series configured Significance Testing Significance series configured Ranking Ranking enabled Indice Value and base series Threshold Masking Threshold enabled Header logos A Logo series measure in Additional Series, or a Header Logos lookup

SDM Xtended Table needs at least: Row field(s): Categories for table rows — as many levels as you need Column field(s): Categories for table columns — as many levels as you need Value field: Numerical data (usually for mean table) or any categorical variable or measure (usually for percentage table). info Tip: You do not need to prepare specific measure, unless you need to weigth your data. For percentage tables, you can use any categorical field (e.g., Product, Region, Gender, Age class, Segment...) or a measure that returns categorical data. For mean tables, use numerical fields (e.g., Sales, Revenue, Age). Example dataset: Product Region Sales Product A North 15,000 Product A South 12,000 Product B North 18,000 Product B South 14,000 With this dataset you can create: a cross-tab showing sales distribution of products across regions, in this case, drop any of "Product" or "Region" column in the "value" field and select "Count" measure in the "Values" field. a mean table showing average sales per product and region, in this case, drop "Sales" column in the "value" field and select "Average" measure in the "Values" field.

Add the SDM Xtended Table visual to your report canvas In the Visualizations pane: Drag one or more fields to Rows (e.g., "Product"); each extra field adds a row level Drag one or more fields to Columns (e.g., "Region"); each extra field adds a column level Drag a measure to Values (e.g., "Sales"), select 'count' for percentage or 'average' for mean table. Select the appropriate table type in Visual properties Your table appears!

In the format panel, you can immediately: Table Type: Switch between "Percentage" or "Mean" Show Measure: Toggle Value, vertical/horizontal percentages, indice buttons Select series usage: Configure multiple value series (e.g., count, mean, std. dev., base, unweighted base...) Show Totals: Add row and column totals, and sub-totals level by level Table Headers: Open the ⚙ Column Headers / Row Headers editors to format each level (see Table Headers) Formatting: Change theme, fonts and colors The default format is a 'custom' basic simple table format: With two click, you can change to other pre-defined styles and color theme like: Classic Indigo: Modern Sunset: Market Research Forest: Scientific Indigo: Or customize your own style: See Styling Your Table for more details.​
Best for survey data, response rates, market share Set Table Type → "Percentage" Check Vertical percentage (% within each column) Check Show total column Enable Zebra rows for readability
Best for averages, performance metrics Set Table Type → "Mean" Configure Mean Series in data properties Add Count Series for sample size Optional: Add Standard Deviation for analysis

Best for highlighting differences in survey data Configure as Percentage Analysis In Significance settings: Set Significance 1 to "All columns" or "Item vs other" Set Significance Level to "95%" Select Font Color for display Significant differences appear highlighted

Best for brand grids or any list of items rated by the same respondents Put the items on the last level of your columns (or rows) In the ⚙ header editor of that level, set Sample across items to "Shared" (or "Native" if your model provides the sub-total measure) Totals then use the real sample size instead of adding the bases of every item (and, with Shared or Native, so do the significance tests against the rest of the row) — see Sample Across Items

Q: My data doesn't appear in the table A: Check that you've assigned values to Rows, Columns, and at least one Value field. Q: Can I show multiple metrics? A: Yes! Drag multiple measures to Values and configure series in settings. Q: How do I add hierarchies? A: Drag multiple fields to Rows or Columns to create hierarchical levels. There is no fixed limit on the number of levels; format each one from the Table Headers editors. Q: Is there a data limit? A: SDM Xtended Table follows Power BI's native limits (~1M rows visual-level). Ready to go deeper? Check out the complete reference guide or explore real-world use cases!

History of SDM Xtended Table. The visual is new (first builds in October 2026) and is independent from CrossTable: it has its own identifier, its own versioning and is not a drop-in replacement for it.

Layout controls move into the header editors, and the tooltip can replay a significance test. Editors organized in sections. Each level block of the ⚙ Column Headers and Row Headers editors is now split into Header, Sub-total and Layout sections. See Table Headers. Width and height per level. New Width (last column level) and Height of each group of this level (any row level) fields: Auto, Distribute equally, Minimal or Fixed (px). They replace the Row height (px) Table option. See Size. Gap per level. One Gap before each group (px) field per level, in standard mode as in Tile mode, at any column or row level. It replaces Row group spacing (Table options) and Group gap, Sub-group gap and Row gap (Tile mode), which no longer exist. A column separator is centered in the gap. See Gaps between groups. Forbid horizontal scroll. New Table option that fits the table in the visual width; long column titles are cut as chosen by the per-level Title cut field. Freeze left column is then hidden. See Table Options. Tooltip. New Tested & compared values content, and the Weighted base and Compared base lines also show the effective bases when the separate effective variance method is used. See Cell Tooltip. Native sample. Sub-totals of a Native level are now also read from the measure in percentage tables (not only in mean tables), falling back to the sum of the items when the measure is BLANK. See Sample Across Items. Existing reports that used the removed options (Row height, Row group spacing, Tile mode gaps) fall back to the defaults: re-enter the values in the editors.

First release line of SDM Xtended Table. N levels of rows and columns. Calculations (percentages, bases, significance, sorting) stay computed per sub-table, whatever the number of row levels. Table Headers card. The ⚙ Column Headers and Row Headers editors replace the Top level / Sub level / Row header format cards: one block per level, without ceiling. They hold the level's font and background, its Logo series, the show choice, the per-level show sub-total choice and, for rows, the layout (side column or full-width band) and a free additional CSS field. See Table Headers. Additional Series role and Header Logos lookup. They replace the Logo Lv1–Lv3 / Row Logo Lv1–Lv2 roles. See Logos in Headers. Per-level sub-totals. Show sub-total is chosen per column level and is on by default at every level. See Totals & Subtotals. Sample across items. A per-level property (Disjoint / Shared / Native) replaces Multiple answer and Rows are repeated items, which no longer exist. See Sample Across Items. Cell Rules accept rowN / colN identifiers for any N. Carried over from CrossTable: percentage and mean tables, Cell Percentage, significance tests (including the separate effective variance method), Ranking, Tile Mode, thresholds and masking, Global Threshold panel, cell Tooltip, transparent background, Excel export. Not included: Data Bar, Data Line and Gap Mode (see CrossTable InCell Charts).

SDM Xtended Table (Socio Data Management Xtended Table for Power BI) is a specialized Power BI custom visual built for creating and analyzing cross-tabulation tables (also known as contingency tables or crosstabs). It keeps everything that makes the CrossTable engine valuable for survey and market-research work, and removes its structural limits: any number of row levels and any number of column levels, each one formatted from a dedicated editor. It goes far beyond simple data grids by providing: Hierarchical table structures with as many levels of rows and columns as your analysis needs Statistical analysis capabilities including multiple significance testing Advanced formatting options to highlight key insights Professional styling for reports and presentations Flexible data aggregation supporting both percentages and means Interactive filtering through row and column selection

SDM Xtended Table is ideal for: Scientific Market Research Professionals: Analyze survey data with deep breakdowns (country > wave > brand > item…) Data Analysts: Create multi-dimensional analysis tables with statistical rigor Business Intelligence Teams: Build professional dashboards and reports Statistical Consultants: Perform complex cross-tabulations with significance tests Corporate Reporting: Generate polished, formatted tables for executive presentations

Cell Rules let you decorate individual cells (color, label, or full CSS) based on conditions you write directly in the visual — no DAX measure required. You type a list of rules in the Cell rules text box (Format pane → Cell Rules). Each rule is a condition : output pair. For every cell, the visual evaluates the rules top to bottom on the values it has already computed (percentages, index, base, mean, significance) and on the row/column header labels, and applies the output of the first rule that matches. Why not a DAX measure anymore? The previous version relied on a Cell Rules DAX measure that had to reproduce the visual's own calculations (vertical %, side-by-side recomputations, per-scale means…). That is impossible to replicate faithfully in DAX. The engine now runs inside the visual, directly on the numbers it displays, so a rule always sees exactly what the user sees. The old Cell Rules data-role field has been removed.

condition : output condition : output default : output One rule per line. Everything left of the first : is the condition; everything to the right is the output. The first matching rule wins (evaluation stops there). default matches everything — use it as a catch-all (put it last). Blank lines and lines starting with // are ignored (comments). // Frequency traffic light pctV < 0.10 : #FF4444;Low pctV < 0.20 : #FF8888;Mid pctV < 0.30 : #8888FF;Good default : #4488FF;Excellent A compilation status is shown under the box: ✅ 4 rule(s) applied, or ❌ Line 3: <message> if a rule is malformed.
A condition is a boolean expression combining comparisons with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses.

These come straight from the visual's own calculations: Variable Meaning Scale pctV Vertical percentage (share of the column) fraction 0–1 (0.33 = 33 %) pctH Horizontal percentage (share of the row) fraction 0–1 cellPct Cell percentage (value / the cell's own base) fraction 0–1 indice Index vs. the level subtotal base 100 (100 = average) value Cell value: count (frequency tables) or mean (mean tables) raw base Weighted base raw avg Mean (mean tables only) raw signif1 First significance test 1 = higher, -1 = lower, 0 = not significant signif2 Second significance test 1 / -1 / 0 Operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Percentages are fractions pctV, pctH and cellPct are stored as fractions, not percentages. Write pctV < 0.10 for "below 10 %", not pctV < 10. (indice on the other hand is on a base-100 scale.) value > 100 AND signif1 = -1 AND pctV < 0.333 : #E63946;Rare & low indice >= 120 : #2E86AB;Over-represented

Test the label of the row/column header at a given level. Level numbering is outermost = 1. Variable Refers to col1, col2, col3, … colN Column header at level 1 / 2 / 3 / … N (top → down). There is no upper limit: use as many as the table has column levels colX Any column level (matches if at least one level matches) row1, row2, … rowN Row header at level 1 / 2 / … N (outer → inner), no upper limit rowX Any row level In tables with several row levels, the outer levels (row1, row2…) name the sub-tables and the last level is the row label itself. In a simple table (one row level), row1 is the visible row label. Operators (all case-insensitive): Operator Meaning CONTAINS "x" Label contains the substring x IN ("a","b","c") Label equals one of the listed values = / != Label equals / differs from a value Quote text with special characters String literals that contain spaces or parentheses must be quoted: row1 CONTAINS "(4)". Without quotes, the parentheses break parsing. Also, the substring must appear literally — CONTAINS "(10)" does not match note sur 10) (there is no ( right before 10); use CONTAINS "sur 10)" instead. col1 = "Total" : #eeeeee;Total column colX CONTAINS "Framatome" : color:#0a7 row1 IN ("BRAND1","BRAND2","BRAND99") : #0088FF;Target Numeric vs. text operators A numeric operator (<, >, …) on a header variable, or CONTAINS on a numeric variable, simply evaluates to false (no error). On colX/rowX, a condition is true if at least one level satisfies it (OR semantics).

The Measure content dropdown (Format pane → Cell Rules settings) decides how each rule's output string is interpreted. For every mode except Custom CSS, the output is #color;label, split on the first ;: Output Interpretation #RRGGBB or #RGB or rgb(...) A color Any text A label #RRGGBB;Label text Color and label (label may contain more ;) Mode Uses Effect Cell background color color Fills the cell background Text color color Colors the cell text Label only label Prepends a label to the cell Label + cell background color + label Background + label Label + text color color + label Text color + label Label + badge color + label Colored badge (shape set by Badge shape) + value Custom CSS free CSS (+ optional label) See below // Mode: Label + badge avg >= 8 : #27AE60;Excellent avg >= 6 : #F39C12;Good avg >= 4 : #E74C3C;Poor

In Custom CSS mode, the output is a raw CSS declaration block, optionally followed by | label. This gives full control: text color that adapts to the background, bold/underline, alignment, gradients, shadows… // Mode: Custom CSS avg < 2.6 AND row1 CONTAINS "sur 4)" : background:#E50158;color:#fff;font-weight:bold | Alert avg < 5.5 AND row1 CONTAINS "sur 10)" : background:#E50158;color:#fff;font-weight:bold | Alert default : background:#EEE;color:#333;text-align:right CSS uses ; as its separator, so in this mode the ; no longer splits color/label — the label (if any) goes after a |. Every declaration is applied with !important, so a rule reliably overrides the default cell/row styling (alternating rows, cell format…).

User CSS is sanitized before being applied, and applied only through the CSSOM (style.setProperty), never as HTML — so it cannot execute JavaScript and cannot load external resources. The sanitizer rejects any declaration whose value contains url(...), image-set(...), expression(...), backslash escapes, at-rules (@…), </>, braces or comments. What still works Gradients (linear-gradient(...)), calc(), rgb()/hsl(), vendor prefixes, text decoration, alignment, shadows — none of these need url(), so they all pass. Only external-resource and code-execution vectors are blocked, keeping the visual certification-safe.

Setting: Activate Cell Rules — Type: Toggle — Default: Off Master switch. When off, no rule is evaluated and no decoration is applied. Setting: Badge shape — visible when mode is Label + badge Shape Appearance Circle Fully rounded pill Square Sharp rectangular badge Rounded Square Rectangle with slightly rounded corners Compatibility with Ranking badges Cell Rules badges and Ranking badges are cumulative — both can appear in the same cell (the Cell Rules badge is placed first).

Rules are evaluated at the very end of the pipeline, after all calculations and after masking: a masked cell is never rendered, so no rule runs on it. If a threshold empties a cell's displayed content, rules still apply (the underlying numbers are still available). Rules apply to data cells and to subtotal / total columns (they all go through the same render path). colX on a grand-total column is empty, but numeric conditions and rowN still work there. The Base / Total rows (Base, Unweighted base…) are out of scope — they bypass the rule engine.

Some modes are mutually exclusive because they write the same visual property. On conflict, the grid is not rendered and an error is shown. Conflict Reason Cell Rules (background) + Ranking (color mode) Both write cell background Cell Rules (background) + Significance (background mode) Both write cell background Cell Rules (text color) + Significance (font color mode) Both write cell text color Ranking (color mode) + Significance (background mode) Both write cell background To resolve: disable one feature or switch to a non-overlapping mode. Significance shown as icons or borders never conflicts. Custom CSS is not conflict-checked Because Custom CSS can set any property, it is not part of the automatic conflict detection — you are responsible for avoiding clashes with Ranking/Significance colors.

Same table, some rows scored /4 and others /10 (marker in the row label). // Mode: Cell background color pctV >= 0.30 : #27AE60 pctV >= 0.15 : #F39C12 default : #E74C3C
// Mode: Label + cell background col1 IN ("Framatome","EDF") AND indice >= 120 : #2E86AB;Key account

The status shows ❌ Line N: Expected ')' found '…' A value or operand is missing on that line (e.g. avg < AND … — no number after <). The parser consumed the next keyword as the missing value. Complete the condition. A header rule never matches The searched text must appear literally in the label and be quoted if it contains spaces/parentheses. Remember CONTAINS "(10)" ≠ note sur 10). A percentage rule never matches pctV/pctH are fractions (0–1). Use pctV < 0.10, not pctV < 10. Custom CSS: background doesn't change (normal mode) Already handled — every Custom CSS declaration is applied with !important, so it overrides the default background. If you edited rules, reload the visual to pick up the change. A url(...) in my CSS is ignored That is intentional: external resources are stripped for certification safety. Use gradients or inline colors instead. Decoration appears on some cells but not others Expected — a cell where no rule matches (and no default is set) is left undecorated.

Enable users to interact with your table by selecting rows or columns headers. This feature allows end-users to filter other page visuals using the SDM Xtended Table visualization. Selection in SDM Xtended Table

There is two available options to enable or disable selection feature: Right click on the table → Enable Selection In the formatting pane, under Table Format section, toggle on or off Enable Selection.

Power BI does not permit filtering multiple variables at the same time. However, users can select multiple rows or columns within the same variable by holding the Ctrl (or Cmd on Mac) key while clicking on the headers.

To clear the current selection: Click on the top left corner cell. Or click again on the selected row/column while holding the Ctrl (or Cmd) key. Right click on the table → Clear Selection. Disable selection (see previous section).

When a row or column is selected: The selected header highlights with a distinct cell border color Other visuals in your report respond to the selection Create interactive dashboards where users control what data displays Combine with slicers and other Power BI features

Data Size: Very large tables (1000+ rows) may have performance impact Nested Hierarchies: Selection on multi-level hierarchies may behave differently Performance: Complex cross-filtering with many connected visuals may be slow

Q: Selection doesn't trigger other visuals to update A: Check Power BI cross-filtering settings. Ensure other visuals have cross-filter enabled. Q: Users can't multi-select rows/columns A: Multi-select depends on browser and Power BI version. Single selection always works. Q: Selected row/column doesn't highlight A: Check that Enable Selection is turned on in formatting panel Q: Selection performance is slow A: Large tables (1000+ rows) may be slow. Consider data aggregation or pagination. For more help, see the Quick Start Guide.

Control the fundamental display behavior of your table including hover effects, row striping, borders, freezing panes, and display precision. Settings Location These settings live in the Table Format card of the SDM Xtended Table format pane, in the Table Options group.
Table Options control how your table behaves and displays data without changing the styling or colors. These are the foundational display settings.

Setting: Highlight row on hover Type: Toggle Default: On Highlights the entire row when your cursor moves over it. Use cases: Interactive dashboards Reports where users will hover to explore Tables with many columns (helps track which row you're in) Example: Normal: | Region | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Hover: | Region | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | ← Entire row highlighted

Setting: Zebra rows Type: Toggle Default: On Alternates row background colors for easier reading. Visual effect: Row 1: White background Row 2: Light gray background Row 3: White background Row 4: Light gray background ... Benefits: Helps readers track across wide tables Improves readability for people with dyslexia Makes data-dense tables easier to scan When to disable: Very narrow tables (few columns) When custom styling already provides good contrast

Setting: Table border Type: Toggle Default: On Shows or hides all cell and table borders. When off, the table renders without any grid lines, giving a clean, minimal look. Significance borders (.sigBordPlus / .sigBordMinus) are preserved regardless of this setting. When to enable (default): Standard reporting where grid lines help readability Dense tables where borders guide the eye across columns When to disable: Tile mode designs (borders already absent per tile) Minimalist dashboards where whitespace replaces structure Embedding a table inside a styled card or frame note Disabling borders does not affect the significance highlight borders — those remain visible to preserve data interpretation.

Setting: Show % symbol Type: Toggle Default: On Controls whether the "%" character appears after percentage values. Examples: On: 45%, 68.5% Off: 45, 68.5 Use cases: Keep On for general reporting (clearer meaning) Turn Off for data-dense tables where space is limited

Setting: Precision Type: Number (0-5) Default: 1 Number of decimal places for percentage display. Common settings: Precision Example Use Case 0 45% Executive summaries, simple reporting 1 45.2% Standard business reporting (most common) 2 45.23% Detailed analysis, research 3+ 45.234% Scientific/academic work Tips: Higher precision = larger numbers in cells (may affect readability) Lower precision = cleaner look but less detail Match precision to your audience's needs
Freezing keeps certain rows/columns visible while scrolling, essential for navigating large tables.

Setting: Forbid horizontal scroll Type: Toggle Default: Off Fits the table into the width of the visual: the data columns shrink instead of overflowing, so no horizontal scrollbar appears. Because a column can no longer widen to fit its title, long column titles are cut — choose how with the Title cut field of each column level in the Column Headers editor (one line + ellipsis, two lines + ellipsis, or as many lines as needed). Good to know: While it is on, the Freeze left column setting is hidden and has no effect (there is nothing to scroll horizontally). The width of the data columns still follows the Width field of the last column level (see Size); when the columns cannot fit, they are scaled down uniformly (never below 30 px).

Setting: Freeze left column Type: Toggle Default: On Keeps the row labels (leftmost column) visible while scrolling horizontally. Hidden — and ignored — while Forbid horizontal scroll is on. When enabled: You scroll left/right through data columns Row labels stay visible on the left Easy to identify which row you're looking at When to disable: Table fits on screen (no horizontal scroll needed) First column should scroll with the rest Example: Frozen left: ┌─────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐ │ Product (F) │ Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 ... (scroll) │ │ Product A │ 100 120 115 130 │ │ Product B │ 85 92 98 105 │ └─────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

Setting: Freeze top row Type: Toggle Default: On Keeps column headers visible while scrolling vertically. When enabled: You scroll up/down through rows Headers stay visible at top Easy to know which column you're looking at When to disable: Table fits on screen (no vertical scroll needed) Headers should scroll with the rest Example: ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Region │ Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 (F) │ ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┤ │ North │ 1000 1100 1050 1200 │ │ South │ 800 920 950 1050 │ │ East │ 1200 1300 1250 1400 │ │ ....... │ ... (scroll down) ... │ └─────────┴──────────────────────────┘ Best Practice Keep both freezing options On for tables larger than your screen. Disable only if your table is small enough to fit completely.

Setting: Row title fixed width Type: Text input Format: Any valid CSS width (200px, 20%, 15em) Default: Empty (automatic sizing) Set a fixed width for the row labels column instead of letting it auto-size. Use cases: Consistent layouts: When creating multiple tables with same row structure Visual alignment: Aligning tables vertically across multiple reports Space control: Limiting label space when labels are very long Examples: /* Fixed pixel width */ Row Title Fixed Width: 250px /* Fixed percentage */ Row Title Fixed Width: 25% /* Em units (relative to font size) */ Row Title Fixed Width: 20em Tips: Leave empty for automatic sizing (recommended for most cases) Use when labels are consistent across reports Test that labels aren't cut off if using fixed widths Percentage widths are relative to total table width When to Use Fixed Width This is particularly useful when you have the same column variables but different row variables across multiple tables, maintaining visual consistency.

In SDM Xtended Table, the size of columns and rows and the gaps between groups are no longer Table options: they are set level by level in the ⚙ Column Headers and Row Headers editors, in the Layout section of each level. This replaces the former Row height (px) and Row group spacing settings (and the Tile mode Group gap, Sub-group gap and Row gap settings), which no longer exist. You want to… Where Give every data row a given height, or make rows fill the visual height Row Headers editor → last level → Layout → Height of each group of this level (details) Set the width of the data columns (equal, fixed, minimal) Column Headers editor → last level → Layout → Width (details) Leave a vertical gap between two sub-tables (one country, one wave…) Row Headers editor → the level of the sub-tables → Layout → Gap before each group (details) Leave a horizontal gap before each group of columns Column Headers editor → the level → Layout → Gap before each group (details)

Setting: Show column header Type: Toggle Default: On Show or hide the whole column header area entirely. To hide only one column header level (and keep the others), use the Show this header field of that level in the Column Headers ⚙ editor instead. When to keep enabled (most cases): Users need to identify columns Multiple hierarchical levels When to disable: Table is part of a dashboard with clear context Column labels are already provided elsewhere Space is extremely limited Headers are obvious from surrounding documentation Example - Headers Hidden: Before (Header On): After (Header Off): ┌──────┬─────┬─────┐ ┌──────┬─────┬─────┐ │ Item │ Q1 │ Q2 │ │ 100 │ 120 │ 115 │ ├──────┼─────┼─────┤ ├──────┼─────┼─────┤ │ A │ 100 │ 120 │ → │ 85 │ 92 │ 98 │ │ B │ 85 │ 92 │ │ 45 │ 52 │ 48 │ └──────┴─────┴─────┘ └──────┴─────┴─────┘

Fine-tune fonts, colors, and backgrounds for specific table elements to create highly customized designs or match brand guidelines exactly. Settings Location Data cells are styled in the Cell format group of the Table Format card. Column and row headers are styled per level in the Table Headers card, through two ⚙ editors (Column Headers / Row Headers) — see Table Headers. Differences with CrossTable CrossTable has fixed Top-Level Column Header, Sub-Level Column Header and Row header format cards, limited to two or three levels. SDM Xtended Table replaces them with one block per header level, with no limit on the number of levels, in the Table Headers editors. The Cell format card below works exactly like CrossTable's.

Custom Element Formatting allows you to control individual elements independently: Column Headers: one formatting block per column level (level 1 = outermost), set in the Column Headers ⚙ editor Row Headers: one formatting block per row level, set in the Row Headers ⚙ editor Cell Format: data cells containing values, set in the Cell format card Each element can have its own font, size, weight, and color settings.

Element Where When the theme is Custom When the theme is Modern / Classic / Scientific / Market Research Cell format Cell format card, toggle Override cell style Forced ON (hidden) — the Custom theme always uses these settings Visible. OFF (default) = theme's built-in cell style. ON = your settings override the theme. Column / Row header levels Table Headers ⚙ editors, field Header colors Always available Always available. Inherit from theme (default) lets the theme decide the level's colors; Custom overrides them. This means you can pick any predefined theme (e.g. Modern) and still customize only the data cells, or only a given header level, without dropping back to the fully manual Custom theme. Surgical overrides Each override is independent. You can keep the theme's stylish headers and just bump the cell font size, or restyle a single header level and leave everything else on the theme.

Every header level (columns or rows) has its own formatting block in the matching ⚙ editor: Header colors (inherit or custom background and font color), font family and size, bold / italic / underline, an optional logo, and — for column levels — a sub-total column style and a column separator. Rows levels also carry a Row layout (side column or full-width banner). 👉 The complete field list is in Table Headers. Default styling (a level without any block): the active style theme decides — typically Arial 11pt bold, with the theme's header background and text color. Use cases for customization: Make the outermost level more prominent (larger, bolder) and the inner levels lighter Match brand colors, level by level Give each level of a deep hierarchy its own visual weight In Tile Mode: keep a solid background on row headers while data tiles float Sticky behavior preserved The background you set on a row level is preserved by sticky-column behavior (when row labels stay frozen on horizontal scroll). The visual will not turn transparent on scroll.

Data cells containing actual values (numbers, percentages, etc.). Default styling: Font: Consolas (monospace for alignment) Size: 11pt Bold: No Background: inherited from theme Text Color: inherited from theme Text alignment: Center Activation: requires the Override cell style toggle to be ON (default OFF on Modern/Classic/Scientific/Market Research; forced ON on Custom). Use cases for customization: Change to more readable font (Arial, Calibri) Make certain values stand out Match data cell styling to headers Force a specific font on top of a predefined theme Tile Mode interaction When Tile Mode is ON, the background defined here is not applied to the data cell — the Tile background (in the Tile Mode card) governs the tile color instead. Fonts and font colors still apply through the tile, so text styling works unchanged.

Setting: Font family Type: Dropdown selection Common options: Arial, Calibri, Verdana, Consolas, Times New Roman, Georgia Recommendations by Use Case​ Font Style Use Case Arial Clean, modern, sans-serif Professional reports, most uses Calibri Modern, readable, sans-serif Business documents, modern look Verdana Large x-height, readable, sans-serif Web, accessibility, easy reading Consolas Monospace, aligned numbers Technical data, precise alignment Times New Roman Traditional, serif Formal, academic, traditional Georgia Serif, readable, elegant Formal, elegant, book-like Accessibility notes: Sans-serif fonts (Arial, Calibri) are more readable for data Avoid decorative/script fonts Serif fonts acceptable for formal headers only

Setting: Font size Type: Number Range: 8pt - 28pt Defaults: Headers: 11pt Cells: 11pt Recommended hierarchy: Column level 1: 12-14pt (largest, most prominent) Deeper column levels: 11-12pt (medium, decreasing) Cell data: 10-11pt (smallest, main focus on data) Tips for sizing: Headers 1-2pt larger than cells Smaller fonts = more data visible, less readable Larger fonts = cleaner look, less data visible Consider your audience (executives prefer larger) Match your brand guidelines

Bold​ Makes text heavier/darker. Recommended usage: ✅ Headers (always bold for prominence) ✅ Important values or totals ❌ Regular data cells (reduces readability) Italic​ Slightly slanted text. Recommended usage: ✅ Subtotals or secondary values ✅ Footnotes or notes ❌ Main data cells (harder to read) Underline​ Line under text. Recommended usage: ✅ Totals row (visual separator) ✅ Important headers ❌ Regular data (unnecessary decoration) Best practices: Use sparingly for emphasis Don't combine more than 2 styles Ensure sufficient contrast with background
The color of the text itself. Format: Hex color code or color picker Examples: #000000 = Black #FFFFFF = White #333333 = Dark gray #2E5090 = Navy blue #006633 = Dark green
The color behind the text. Format: Hex color code or color picker Examples: #FFFFFF = White #F5F5F5 = Light gray #E8F4F8 = Light blue #2E5090 = Navy blue

Setting: Transparent background Type: Toggle Default: Off Makes the table background transparent (cells, theme card and shadow) so the report canvas shows through the visual. Significance, ranking and conditional-rule backgrounds are kept.

Setting: Include headers Type: Toggle Default: Off With Transparent background on, also makes the row and column headers transparent. By default headers stay opaque so frozen headers remain readable while scrolling. note Header levels with a Custom background in the Table Headers editors keep their own color.

Setting: Row title text alignment Type: Dropdown Options: Left, Center, Right Default: Left Controls how row labels (left column) are aligned horizontally. Options: Alignment Example Best For Left Standard, most readable Center Formal, numbers-like appearance Right Technical, numeric labels
Theme: Modern Color: Blue or Slate Cell text: 10-11pt Row align: Left Result: Clean, professional, trustworthy

When "Custom" is selected, you have full control to match any brand or preference. Refer to Custom Element Formatting for detailed font and color settings. Best for: Brand matching (company colors) Non-standard designs Accessibility requirements Experimental layouts Extending Custom Theme To fully customize fonts and colors per element, combine Custom style with the Cell format card (data cells) and the per-level Table Headers editors (column and row headers).
Themes are applied in this order (later overrides earlier): Style Theme (base) Color Theme (palette) Cell text size Row alignment Custom Element Formatting and per-level Table Headers (if applied)

Start with a Theme: Don't start with Custom - choose a theme that's close Consistent Palettes: Theme colors are designed to work together - use them Test Your Audience: Show sample tables to your audience before finalizing Light vs. Dark: Choose Light for printed reports, Dark for digital dashboards Accessibility: Avoid low-contrast combinations (e.g., Yellow with Light) Brand Alignment: If using Custom, ensure it matches your brand guidelines

Use Custom Element Formatting if you need to: Change fonts per element (headers vs. cells) Style each header level differently (see Table Headers) Fine-tune specific colors Add bold/italic to headers Match exact brand color codes

Render each cell (or sub-cell) as a detached tile with rounded corners, optional drop shadow, configurable padding. Group and row gaps are set per level (see below). Tile Mode transforms the table from a classic grid into a card-like layout while keeping the underlying HTML <table> structure intact — all existing features (significance, ranking, thresholds, sticky columns, sorting, masking…) continue to work. Settings Location These settings live in the Tile mode group of the Table Format card.

Tile Mode is a non-destructive visual layer: OFF (default): classic grid rendering, no change to existing behavior. ON: each cell becomes a detached tile with its own background, rounded corners, shadow, and configurable spacing. The mode works across all five style themes (Modern, Classic, Scientific, Market Research, Custom).

Setting: Tile mode (toggle) Default: Off When enabled, the whole tile system activates: cell wrapping, sub-cell tiling, gaps, gradient backgrounds for significance, etc. When disabled, the table renders exactly as before — no impact whatsoever.
Type: Number (px) Default: 8 Rounded corner radius of each tile. Larger values create softer, more "card-like" tiles. Set to 0 for square tiles.
Type: Number (px) Default: 4 Internal left/right padding inside each tile. Increases the horizontal breathing room around the value.

Type: Number (px) Default: 4 Internal top/bottom padding inside each tile. Use a higher value (e.g. 8-12) to create visually taller tiles. Independent H/V padding Horizontal and vertical padding are independent. A common pattern is a smaller horizontal padding with a larger vertical one to make tiles slightly taller without making them wider.
Setting: Drop shadow (toggle) Default: On Adds a soft drop shadow below each tile for a floating, card-like effect.

Type: Number (1 to 30) Default: 6 Controls the shadow's depth and spread: Value Effect 1-3 Very subtle — barely perceptible 4-8 Soft — good for clean layouts 10-15 Pronounced — clear floating effect 20-30 Strong — dramatic, presentation-grade The shadow is composed of two layers (a wide soft layer and a tighter dense layer) so it stays elegant even at high intensities.

Setting: Tile background (color) Default: #ffffff (white) Background color of non-significant tiles. Tiles that are significant (positive or negative) use the significance colors instead — see Significance settings.

Type: Text Default: -1 (auto) Controls the width of every tile in the table. Two modes: Value Behavior -1, empty, or auto Auto-equalize: every tile gets the width of the widest natural cell (measured after rendering). Recommended when displaying logos or when column headers are hidden — otherwise columns can end up with very different widths. 60, 60px, 5em, 2.5rem Explicit: forces an exact width on every tile. A bare number is interpreted as pixels. Invalid values (e.g. abc) fall back to auto. When to use explicit width When column headers are hidden (Show column header = off): tiles have no header to constrain their width, and they may stretch differently per row. Use auto or explicit to enforce consistency. When logos of different sizes appear in headers: auto width measures each cell after image decoding and aligns them. When you need very compact columns: set an explicit small width (e.g. 45px).

Gaps create visual breathing room between tiles. They are implemented via transparent borders, which add real physical width without altering the tile content. All horizontal gaps are split symmetrically between the two adjacent tiles (half on the right of the previous tile, half on the left of the next).
Type: Number (px) Default: 4 Gap between sub-cells inside a multi-value cell (when 2, 3 or 4 measures are displayed per cell). Higher values clearly separate the value, percentage, indice, etc.

Horizontal gaps between groups of columns and vertical gaps between groups of rows are no longer Tile mode settings. They are set with the Gap before each group (px) field of each level, in the Layout section of the ⚙ Column Headers and Row Headers editors, and they apply in tile mode and in standard mode alike. This replaces the former Group gap, Sub-group gap and Row gap settings, which no longer exist, and removes the old limit to two column levels: any column or row level can carry its own gap. For a tile look equivalent to the former defaults, set a gap of about 16 on column level 1 and about 8 on column level 2. The gap is also applied before the sub-total column of the level (see Show sub-total column in the Column Headers editor). For vertical airiness, set a gap on the last row level: it is then added between two consecutive rows (half below each row, half above the next, so 8 gives an 8-pixel visual gap).
documents.s: Gaps between groups — now per level

documents.t: Tile Mode is designed to coexist with the rest of the visual:

Significance backgrounds (positive/negative) are applied to the inner tile, not the <td> placeholder — so the colored area respects the tile's rounded corners and shadow. In multi-value cells, the colored sub-tile is the one carrying the significant measure (e.g. the pctV sub-tile). You can combine Tile Mode with gradient significance backgrounds: see the Significance settings — the gradient is applied to the tile itself.

In single-value tile cells, ranking visuals are applied to the inner tile: Rank label (numeric badge): positioned against the tile's left edge. Color scale (red→blue / red→green / custom): the gradient color is applied to the tile background, not the transparent <td>. The auto-contrast text color also targets the tile.

In Tile Mode, threshold behavior is friendlier: Mask threshold (cell base below threshold): renders an empty tile (visible card with no content) instead of the --- text used in classic mode. Cleaner visual. Warning threshold: the ⚠️ icon is inserted inside the tile (single-value: before the value; multi-value: in the first sub-tile), not next to it.
When header logos are configured (see Table Headers) and tiles are wider than usual, set Tile width to auto so every tile matches the widest header logo (post-decoding).
Sticky row headers continue to work normally. Their background is preserved by the tile mode CSS (only <td> data cells become transparent placeholders).
The classic side-by-side separator (a 2px border between sub-tables) is kept independent of the per-level gaps.

When you want… Set… Subtle card effect radius 6-8, shadow intensity 4-6, padding 4/4 Strong card effect radius 10-12, shadow intensity 12-18, padding 6/8 Dense layout radius 4, shadow off, padding 2/2, sub-cell gap 2 Airy / dashboard radius 10, shadow 8, padding 6/10; gap 6 on the last row level, gap 24 on column level 1 Magazine-like radius 14, shadow 20, padding 8/12; gap 8 on the last row level, gap 32 on column level 1

If Tile mode is OFF: None of the tile CSS is injected. All tile sliders / colors are ignored (the per-level gaps of the header editors still apply, since they also work in standard mode). The table renders identically to previous versions. This means you can keep your existing reports untouched and only enable Tile Mode where you want the new look.
documents.s: Behavior When Tile Mode Is Off

documents.t: Equalizing tile widths (auto mode): a synchronous measure pass runs after rendering, plus a deferred remeasure when images (logos) finish decoding. The cost is negligible for tables up to a few thousand cells. Shadows: composed of two box-shadow layers per tile. Very high intensities on very large tables can slow down scrolling on low-end devices — use intensities ≤ 20 in production reports with 1000+ cells.

Custom Element Formatting — override fonts/colors per element (works alongside tile mode) Table Headers — per-level header colors, fonts and logos Significance settings — gradient backgrounds use the tile as a target Thresholds — mask/warning behave differently in tile mode Ranking — color scales apply to the inner tile Formatting Overview — all formatting options

The Global Threshold card decides what the visual shows when the table should not be drawn at all. It covers two situations, each with its own message: An empty dataset — a page, report or slicer filter leaves the matrix without a single data row. A test you define — typically "the base is below 30 respondents, do not publish these figures". In both cases the table is replaced by a panel you control: message, alignment, font, text color, background and transparency. Not to be confused with the Thresholds card Thresholds works cell by cell — it warns on, or masks, individual values whose base is too small, and the table is still drawn. Global Threshold works on the whole visual: nothing is drawn at all, only the panel. Hence the name. Replaces Clear on Empty dataset This card supersedes the old Clear on Empty dataset toggle of the Table Contents card, which could only choose between a hard-coded "No data to display" message and a blank screen. See Coming from Clear on Empty dataset.

Global Threshold is available on SDM Xtended Table. The card is identical to the one found in CrossTable and CrossTable InCell Charts (same properties, same behavior, same defaults), but is documented here again so that this section is self-contained. Location: Format pane → Global Threshold card.

Property Description Default Empty Panel Draws the panel when the dataset is empty. Switch it off to render strictly nothing in that case. On Message Text drawn on the panel for an empty dataset. Leave it empty for a completely blank panel. Supports conditional formatting (fx). No Data to display

Property Description Default Conditional Message Text drawn instead of the table when the test below is met. Leave it empty for a completely blank panel. Supports conditional formatting (fx). Not enough data to display Test if Left operand — normally a measure bound through fx (a base, a count of respondents). 0 Is The comparison: >, = or <. < To Right operand — a constant, or a measure through fx. 0

Property Description Default Horizontal Alignment Left, center or right. Center Vertical Alignment Top, middle or bottom. Middle Font Font family, size, and bold / italic / underline. The size supports conditional formatting (fx). Segoe UI, 14 pt Text Color Message color. Supports conditional formatting (fx). #333333 Background Color Fill painted behind the message. Supports conditional formatting (fx). #FFFFFF Transparency Background transparency, 0 % (opaque) to 100 % (invisible). Supports conditional formatting (fx). 100 % :::note Why the background looks like nothing at first Transparency defaults to 100 %, so the panel is transparent out of the box and the report page shows through behind the message. Lower it to make Background Color visible. :::

An empty dataset means the matrix reaches the visual with no data rows at all: a filter — page level, report level, a slicer, a cross-highlight — excludes every respondent or every category. It is not: blank or zero cells inside an otherwise populated table (that is Thresholds or Masking); a missing field binding — that case still shows the usual "Please check that you have at least one Row and one column variable" message. Whatever the card says, the table is never drawn on an empty dataset — no empty "shell" made of a column header and a Base row at 0 — and the Excel export button is never shown, since there would be nothing to export. Power BI is also told that rendering has completed, so the page does not stay stuck in a loading state and Export to PDF or Print does not wait on a visual that will never draw. From there, Empty Panel decides: On (default) — the panel is drawn: the background fill first, then Message at the chosen alignment, in the chosen font and color. Off — nothing is drawn at all. The visual's frame stays in place, empty.

The conditional message answers a different need: there is data, but it must not be published. A base of 12 respondents, a period still being collected, a segment too narrow to be significant — the figures exist, they simply should not be read. The test reads as one sentence: Test if (a measure) Is < To (a value) When it holds, the table is not drawn — exactly as for an empty dataset — and Conditional Message is displayed on the panel instead.

Write the measure that carries the number to test, for instance the unweighted base of the table: Respondents = COUNTROWS ( Answers ) In the Global Threshold card, click the fx button of Test if and bind it to that measure. Set Is to < and To to your publication threshold, for example 30. Type the text in Conditional Message: Sample too small to be published Below 30 respondents, the table disappears behind the message; at 30 or above, it renders normally. The message can carry the figure Conditional Message also carries an fx button, so it can come from a measure and quote the number that triggered it: Threshold Message = "Sample too small to be published (" & [Respondents] & " respondents)"

The conditional message has no on/off property: it applies whenever the test is met. With the shipped defaults — Test if 0, Is <, To 0 — the test is false (0 is not below 0), so the feature stays off until you bind or change something. Keep that in mind when choosing the operator: = with both operands left at 0 would be true, and the visual would show the conditional message on every page.
documents.s: There is no toggle — the test is the switch

documents.t: The two cases never compete: the test is only evaluated when the dataset has rows. An empty dataset always shows Message (or nothing, if Empty Panel is off), never the conditional one. This also removes an awkward edge: on an empty dataset a measure normally returns BLANK(), so a test built on a base measure could not be trusted there anyway.

Left untouched, Message shows No Data to display and Conditional Message shows Not enough data to display. In both cases the visual replaces the text at render time with the translation matching the report's language — the same ten languages the visuals ship with (English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese). As soon as you type your own text, that text is used verbatim, exactly as typed, in every language. A multilingual report therefore either keeps the default messages, or drives them with a measure: Empty Message = VAR ReportLanguage = SELECTEDVALUE ( Languages[Code], "en" ) RETURN SWITCH ( ReportLanguage, "fr", "Aucune donnée pour cette sélection", "de", "Keine Daten für diese Auswahl", "No data for this selection" ) :::caution A measure often returns BLANK on an empty dataset An fx rule is evaluated in the visual's own filter context — the very context that has just been emptied. A measure built on the fact table (a count of respondents, a base) typically returns BLANK() there, and Message then falls back to the typed constant. Build it on a table the filter does not empty (a language or parameter table, a disconnected table), or wrap it in COALESCE / IF ( ISBLANK ( … ) , … ). Conditional Message is not affected: it is only ever shown while the table has rows. ::: Text Color, Background Color, Transparency and the font size accept rules as well, so the panel can change appearance with the situation — a neutral gray for "no collection this month", a warning color for a base below the publication threshold.

The old toggle lived on the Table Contents card and had the opposite polarity. The mapping is: Old — Clear on Empty dataset New — Empty Panel Result Off (default) On (default) The localized "No data to display" message — same as before, now stylable On Off Nothing at all — same as before :::warning The old value is not carried over The removed setting is a clean cut: reports that had Clear on Empty dataset switched on now fall back to the new default, which shows the message. Switch Empty Panel off in those reports to get the blank screen back. :::
documents.s: Coming from Clear on Empty dataset

documents.t: The panel never intercepts clicks: pointer events pass through, so the report page keeps behaving normally underneath. The About icon, the ⚙ gear icons of the editor-only editors, and the Powered by Socio Data Management watermark of the Free edition remain visible above the panel. See Editions. Messages accept line breaks and wrap on the width of the visual; text that exceeds the available height is clipped rather than overflowing. The panel is cleared at the start of every render, so it can never linger over a table that has data again. Data fields stay bound in both cases, and the visual keeps its position and size on the page: as soon as the filters let rows through, or the test stops holding, the table comes straight back — nothing is lost.

A different mechanism from CrossTable CrossTable binds logos through fixed data roles (colLogoLv1…rowLogoLv2) and a dedicated Logos card, capped at three column levels and two row levels. SDM Xtended Table has neither the roles nor the card: logos are configured from the Table Headers card, with no limit on the number of levels.

Logos let you display images inside row and column headers — for example company or brand logos in a competitor comparison, or product icons in a key-account table. In SDM Xtended Table, every row level and every column level can show a logo, whatever the depth of your hierarchy. There are two ways to feed a logo to a header level, both set up from the Table Headers card in the Format pane: Way When to use it Cost Header Logos lookup (⚙ editor, headerLogoLookup) The logo depends only on the header label (a brand, a country…). You map an exact label to a base64 image once, in the editor. None: resolved entirely inside the visual, no query cost. Preferred. Logo series (additionalTable data role) The logo comes from your data model, as a DAX measure returning a base64 image, constant per category. One extra measure evaluated per matrix cell, which can be heavy on large tables. No external URLs Logos are provided as base64 data URIs, never as an external URL. Every image is passed through sanitizeImageDataUri before being rendered, keeping the visual certification-safe.

Everything — which level shows a logo, its size, its display mode, the lookup table and the optional named logo tables — is described on one page: Table Headers — the ⚙ Column Headers / Row Headers editors (per-level logo size and mode), the Header Logos lookup editor, named logo tables and the additionalTable Logo series. For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the logos tutorial in the same section.

CrossTable SDM Xtended Table colLogoLv1/2/3, rowLogoLv1/2 data roles Removed. Use the Header Logos lookup, or the additionalTable role for a Logo series Logos card (Show logos, size and mode per level) Removed. Size and mode are fields of the per-level ⚙ editors in the Table Headers card Max 3 column levels / 2 row levels No cap A CrossTable report is not migrated automatically: SDM Xtended Table is a separate visual, so logos must be set up again with the mechanisms above.

Every logo goes through sanitizeImageDataUri before reaching the DOM: only well-formed data:image/...;base64, URIs of an allowed image type are rendered; anything else is silently dropped. The visual never fetches an image from the network.
Configure which data series (measures) are used for mean (average) calculations, statistical properties, and significance testing in mean tables.

Mean tables display average values rather than percentages or counts. They're used for: Customer satisfaction scores Performance metrics (ratings, scores, times) Financial averages (revenue per customer, average order value) Measurement data (temperature, weight, distance) tip Mean tables are ideal for continuous data where averages and variability matter. Continuous (or numeric) data are indicated within Power Bi with a sigma (Σ) symbol next to the measure name (here under L2 and L5). Example Mean Table: Mean table showing average score of customer recognition by media channel and survey cell warning The component itself DOES NOT calculate means directly. You must provide appropriate measures from your data model for each series (Average, Count, Std Dev, etc.) or a pre-calculated measure for weighted mean. See the Data Model Requirements section for details on creating these measures.

Setting: Mean series Required: Yes Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The primary data series containing the values to be averaged. What It Contains: Individual measurements or scores Pre-calculated means (if aggregated in data model) Weighted average (if using weights) Usually, after having dropped the variable in the 'values' section, you will use the 'Average' function in the dropdown listed measures: You can also create custom DAX measures for more complex mean calculations. Examples: Example 1: Satisfaction Scores Mean Series = AVERAGE(Survey[SatisfactionScore]) Data: - Respondent A: 5 - Respondent B: 4 - Respondent C: 5 Mean = (5 + 4 + 5) / 3 = 4.67 Example 2: Revenue per Customer Mean Series = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Revenue]), DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])) Calculates: Average revenue per unique customer Common Sources: AVERAGE(Table[Metric]) DIVIDE(SUM(Values), COUNT(Records)) Pre-calculated mean field Weighted mean calculation

Setting: Count series Required: For displaying sample size Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The number of observations used to calculate show the sample size. What It Shows: Sample size (n) Number of respondents/records Reliability indicator Why It Matters: Product A: Mean = 4.2, Count = 1000 ✅ Reliable Product B: Mean = 4.8, Count = 5 ❌ Unreliable Same difference (0.6), but Product B has tiny sample Usually, you will use the 'Count' or 'Count(Distinct)' function in the dropdown listed measures: You may also create custom DAX measures for specific counting logic. Examples: Example 1: Simple Count Count Series = COUNTROWS(Survey) Counts: All rows in the table warning using COUNTROWS will count all rows, including one which may NOT take part in the calculation. If your variable contains missing or irrelevant data, use the 'Count Rows' function in the dropdown listed functions. Example 2: Respondent Count Count Series = DISTINCTCOUNT(Survey[RespondentID]) Counts: Unique respondents (not duplicate responses) Example 3: Non-Missing Values Count Series = COUNTROWS(FILTER(Survey, NOT(ISBLANK(Survey[Score])))) Counts: Only records with actual scores Display in Table: Product A Product B Product C Base 1250 980 45 Average 4.2 4.5 3.9 ■ Large sample ▪ Small sample (less reliable)

Setting: Standard deviation series Required: For significance testing and variability analysis Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The measure of variability/spread in the data. This measure is required for significance testing of mean differences. It is never displayed directly in the table but used in calculations behind the scenes.

Setting: Mean series for significance tests Required: Only if using significance tests Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) There is cases where you may need to provide a different mean series for significance testing than the one used for display, reason why the tool proposes this separate setting. Set here the mean values used for statistical significance testing. When It Differs from Mean Series: Display uses weighted means Testing uses unweighted means Different aggregation rules for testing Common Scenarios: Scenario 1: Same as Mean Series (Most Common) Mean Series: AVERAGE(Survey[Score]) Significance Mean Series: AVERAGE(Survey[Score]) Use when: Testing and display use same data Mean table showing same mean series for display and significance testing Scenario 2: Different Series tip To Create a weighted mean, use "New Measure" in Power BI and entrer a DAX formula like: L2_weighted = DIVIDE( SUMX(main, main[L2] * main[Weight]), // Note the SUMX to multiply row by row each L2 value by its Weight SUM(main[Weight]), BLANK() // if divide by Zero ) You will also need to create a weighted standard deviation measure for significance testing. L2_WStdDev = VAR MeanValue = [L2_weighted] RETURN SQRT( DIVIDE( SUMX( main, main[Weight] * POWER(main[L2] - MeanValue, 2) ), SUM(main[Weight]) ) ) Example: Here under are three different settings in the first one the 'Mean Series' is set to a raw mean measure with the 'Significance Mean Series' set the same as count Series. in the second one the 'Mean Series' is still set to a raw mean measure with the 'Significance Mean Series' and 'Count Series' set to the Weighted measures. With these settings, significance use the weighted population and the weighted mean for testing while the display use the raw mean so values remains the same while significance tests are based differently. in the third one the 'Mean Series' is set to a weighted mean measure with the 'Significance Mean Series' set to a raw mean measure and the 'Count Series' set to the raw count measure. With these settings, significance use the raw population and the raw mean for testing while the display use the weighted mean so values differs between display and testing. Mean table showing the same mean series for display (unweighted) and significance testing (unweighted) Mean table showing different mean series for display (weighted) and significance testing (unweighted) Note the difference in the 'Count series' and 'Mean Series for significance tests' Mean table showing different mean series for display (unweighted) and significance testing (weighted) Note the difference in the 'Count series' and 'Mean Series for significance tests' Why Separate?: Research protocols may require unweighted testing Different statistical requirements Regulatory or methodological standards

Setting: Unweighted base series Required: Only when using weighted data Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The raw count of observations before weighting adjustments. Used for unweighted base row only, no calculation is made with it. When to Use: For research transparency To show actual sample sizes

The mean of a sub-total or total column is re-aggregated from its children as a base-weighted mean, Σ(meanᵢ × baseᵢ) / Σ(baseᵢ). When Power BI can supply a native sub-total for your measure at that level (for instance a true weighted DAX mean), the native value is used instead. How the children's bases combine depends on the Sample across items property of the level that groups them (Column Headers / Row Headers editors, ⚙) — see Sample Across Items and Understanding Bases.

1. Mean: Either select 'Average' in the dropdown selection of the continuous variable (raw only) or create a Mean Calculation​ // Simple average MeanScore = AVERAGE(Survey[Score]) // Or weighted average WeightedMean = VAR FilteredData = FILTER(Survey, NOT(ISBLANK(Survey[Score]))) // Define the Sub-Set of Data where 'Score' is present (not necessary if variable is mandatory) DIVIDE( SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Score] * Survey[Weight]), SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Weight]), BLANK() ) 2. Count: Either select 'Count' in the dropdown selection (raw), the 'Sum' function of the weight variable or a Size Calculation​ // Simple count SampleSize = COUNTROWS(Survey) // Or unique respondents RespondentCount = DISTINCTCOUNT(Survey[RespondentID]) // Or non-blank count ValidResponses = COUNTROWS(FILTER(Survey, NOT(ISBLANK(Survey[Score])))) // or Weighted count WeightedCount = SUM(Survey[Weight]) warning You SHOULD NOT Count another variable (like the record ID or respondent ID) as the Average or Std Deviation are calculated upon non-null values of the selected mean variable. 3. Standard Deviation: Either select 'Standard Deviation' in the dropdown selection of the variable or create a Standard Deviation Calculation​ // Sample standard deviation StdDeviation = STDEV.S(Survey[Score]) // Or Weighted standard deviation WeightedStdDev = VAR FilteredData = FILTER(Survey, NOT(ISBLANK(Survey[Score]))) // Define the Sub-Set of Data where 'Score' is present VAR MeanValue = DIVIDE(SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Score] * Survey[Weight]), SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Weight])) RETURN SQRT( DIVIDE( SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Weight] * POWER(Survey[Score] - MeanValue, 2) ), SUMX(FilteredData, Survey[Weight]) ) ) 4. Unweighted Base : This shoud ALWAYS be a raw 'count' or 'Count distinct' function of non-null value of selected mean variable​ UnweightedCount = DISTINCTCOUNT(Survey[Score]) warning You SHOULD NOT Count another variable (like the record ID or respondent ID) as the Mean or Std Deviation are calculated upon non-null values of the selected mean variable.
Question: "Rate your satisfaction (1-5)" Configuration: - Mean Series: "Average Satisfaction Score" - Count Series: "Count of Respondents" - StdDev Series: Not shown
Metric: Employee performance ratings Configuration: - Mean Series: "Average Rating" - Count Series: "Employee Count" - StdDev Series: "Rating Std Dev"

Survey: National satisfaction study (weighted) Configuration: - Mean Series: "Weighted Mean Satisfaction" - Count Series: "Sum of Weights" - StdDev Series: "Satisfaction Std Dev" - Unweighted Base: "Count of Respondents" - Significance Mean: "Unweighted Mean"
Metric: Average revenue per customer Configuration: - Mean Series: "Revenue per Customer" - Count Series: "Customer Count"

Good for: Continuous measurements (temperature, time, money) Rating scales (1-5, 1-10) Satisfaction scores (NPS, CSAT) Performance metrics Financial averages Not Good for: Categorical data (Yes/No, Male/Female) Count data (number of purchases) Percentages/proportions Binary outcomes Use percentage tables instead for: Frequency distributions, category breakdowns

Minimum Sample Sizes: n < 30: Means unreliable, use caution n = 30-100: Acceptable for most purposes n > 100: Reliable means n > 1000: Very stable estimates Impact on Significance: Large samples detect small differences Small samples miss real differences Always consider practical significance
A: Verify Mean Series calculation in a simple visual first Check for filter context issues in DAX Ensure measure aggregates correctly across dimensions
A: Check if counting rows vs distinct IDs Verify weighted vs unweighted count Look for filter context in measure definition
A: Ensure StdDev Series is mapped Check that measure returns values Verify sufficient data points (need n ≥ 2)
