Configure which data series (measures) are used for different calculations in percentage tables. Proper series mapping is essential for accurate percentages, bases, and significance testing.

In Power BI, a series is a measure or calculated field that contains numerical data. For percentage tables, you need to map different series to different purposes: Value Series: The numerator (what you're counting) Base Series: The denominator (what you're dividing by) Additional Series: For significance testing and unweighted bases

Setting: Values series Required: Yes Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The primary data series used to populate cell values. What It Contains: For single response: Count of respondents selecting each option For multiple response: Count of respondents mentioning each item For weighted data: Weighted counts Example: If measuring product preference: Value Series = "Count of Respondents" or Value Series = "Sum(WeightedResponses)" Common Sources: COUNT(ResponseID) SUM(Weight) COUNTROWS(Responses) Pre-calculated measure from your data model

Setting: Base series Required: For accurate percentages Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The denominator used to calculate percentages. What It Contains: Total count of respondents in each column Total population for the segment Weighted base (if using weights) Calculation: Percentage = (Value Series / Base Series) × 100 Example: Column: Male Respondents Value Series: 150 (males who chose Product A) Base Series: 300 (total males) Result: 150 / 300 = 50% Common Sources: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) SUM(Weight) (for weighted base) Pre-calculated base measure Important: Base Series should match the scope of your analysis: For column percentages: Base = column total For row percentages: Base = row total For total percentages: Base = grand total

Setting: Unweighted base series Required: Only if using weighted data Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The raw count of respondents/records before any weighting adjustments. When to Use: Your data is weighted (demographics, quotas, etc.) You need to show actual sample sizes For research transparency What It Shows: Total North South Weighted Base 1000 400 600 Unweighted 950 350 600 ← This row Example: Unweighted Base Series = "COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID)" (Counts actual people, ignoring weights) Why It Matters: Shows actual sample size (reliability indicator) Required for professional research reporting Helps readers understand data confidence

XtendedTable has no global "Multiple answer?" toggle. Whether a question is single- or multiple-answer — and whether items are rated by the same people — is declared per header level with the Sample across items property of the Column Headers / Row Headers editors (⚙, in the Table Headers card). Value Typical use Disjoint (default) Single-answer variables: each respondent falls in exactly one item. Bases add up. Shared Multiple-answer variables, batteries of items rated by the same respondents. Bases do not add up. Native Items shown to partially overlapping subsets of the sample: the sub-total is read from your measure.

Characteristics: Column percentages sum to 100% Each respondent counted once per column Standard cross-tabulation Question: "Which ONE product do you prefer?" Total Male Female Base 1000 480 520 Product A 45% 42% 48% Product B 35% 38% 32% Product C 20% 20% 20% Total 100% 100% 100% ← Sums to 100%

Characteristics: Column percentages may exceed 100% Each respondent can be counted multiple times Base = total respondents (not total mentions) Question: "Which products do you use? (Select all)" Total Male Female Base 1000 480 520 Product A 65% 60% 70% Product B 45% 50% 40% Product C 30% 35% 25% Total 140% 145% 135% ← Can exceed 100% Percentage = (Count of respondents mentioning item / Total respondents) × 100 Set Shared on the level whose items are combined so that totals and sub-totals keep the base of one item instead of summing them, and so that significance tests no longer compare a cell with a "rest of the sample" inflated by the sum of the bases. tip The full explanation, with the DAX pattern required by Native, is in Sample Across Items. See also Understanding Bases.

Setting: Effective base series Required: Only with the Separate (effective base) variance method Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) A ready-made effective base (typically raw N × design effect E, with E = (Σ weights)² / (N × Σ weights²)), used "as is" as the denominator of the proportion variance by that method. P1 and P2 keep coming from the value and base series. See Significance Testing → Variance Method.
These series are used when performing statistical significance tests.

Setting: Significance tests series Required: Only if using significance tests Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The data series used for calculating significance tests. What It Should Contain: Same type of data as Value Series May be identical to Value Series Could be different if testing on different data Common Scenarios: Scenario 1: Same as Value Series Value Series: "Sum(WeightedResponses)" Significance Series: "Sum(WeightedResponses)" Use when: Testing on the same weighted data you're displaying Scenario 2: Different Series Value Series: "Sum(WeightedResponses)" (for display) Significance Series: "Count(Responses)" (for testing) Use when: Display weighted but test unweighted Why Separate?: Research methodologies may require testing on unweighted data Display and testing may use different rules Specialized weighting scenarios

Setting: Base series for significance tests Required: Only if using significance tests Type: Dropdown (lists available measures) The base used for calculating proportions in significance tests. What It Should Contain: Denominator for significance calculations May match Base Series or be different Must align with Significance Series Example: Testing whether males differ from females on Product A preference: Significance Series: Count(Males choosing A) = 150 Base Signif Series: Count(All Males) = 300 Proportion: 150/300 = 0.50 Compare to: Significance Series: Count(Females choosing A) = 180 Base Signif Series: Count(All Females) = 400 Proportion: 180/400 = 0.45 Test: Is 0.50 significantly different from 0.45? Common Configuration: If using weighted data for display but unweighted for testing: Base Series: "Sum(Weight)" (denominator for display %) Base Signif Series: "COUNT(RespondentID)" (denominator for testing)

Best for: Internal analysis, no weighting needed Value Series: COUNT(Responses) Base Series: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) Sample across items: As appropriate (Disjoint / Shared / Native) Significance Series: (same as Value) Base Signif Series: (same as Base)

Best for: Weighted reporting without statistical tests Value Series: SUM(Weight) Base Series: SUM(Weight) Unweighted Base Series: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) Sample across items: As appropriate (Disjoint / Shared / Native)

Best for: Professional research with significance tests Value Series: SUM(WeightedResponse) Base Series: SUM(Weight) Unweighted Base Series: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) Significance Series: COUNT(Response) Base Signif Series: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) Sample across items: As appropriate (Disjoint / Shared / Native)

Best for: Multiple weighting schemes, advanced research Value Series: SUM(DisplayWeight) Base Series: SUM(DisplayWeight) Unweighted Base Series: COUNT(DISTINCT RespondentID) Significance Series: SUM(TestWeight) Base Signif Series: SUM(TestWeight)

For proper percentage tables, ensure your data model includes: 1. Value Measure​ Value = COUNTROWS(Responses) or WeightedValue = SUM(Responses[Weight]) 2. Base Measure​ Base = DISTINCTCOUNT(Responses[RespondentID]) or WeightedBase = CALCULATE(SUM(Responses[Weight]), ALL(Responses[Response])) 3. Unweighted Base (if needed)​ UnweightedBase = DISTINCTCOUNT(Responses[RespondentID]) 4. Significance Measures (if testing)​ SignifValue = COUNTROWS(Responses) SignifBase = DISTINCTCOUNT(Responses[RespondentID])
Single choice question No weighting No significance testing → Value Series: Response count → Base Series: Respondent count → Sample across items: Disjoint
"Select all that apply" question No weighting No significance testing → Value Series: Mention count → Base Series: Respondent count → Sample across items: Shared

Weighted to population Show both weighted and unweighted No significance testing → Value Series: Weighted count → Base Series: Weighted base → Unweighted Base Series: Raw count → Sample across items: As appropriate

Weighted display Unweighted testing Statistical significance → Value Series: Weighted count → Base Series: Weighted base → Unweighted Base Series: Raw count → Significance Series: Unweighted count → Base Signif Series: Unweighted base → Sample across items: As appropriate

Automatically rank cells within each column and visualize rankings with numbers, colors, or gradients.
Setting: Do ranking Type: Toggle Default: Off Turns ranking on/off for all cells in the table.

Setting: Cell value Type: Dropdown Options: Value, Horizontal Percentage, Cell Percentage, Indice Default: Value Which metric to rank by within each column. Cell Percentage (value divided by the cell's own base, see Cell Percentage) can rank differently from Value when bases vary from row to row. info the metric used for ranking DOES NOT need to be displayed in the table. You can rank on one metric while displaying another. tip It is an interesting feature to sort on a specific measure but to rank on another measure like 'Sorting my metric vertical percentage but rank on indice'. note Because Vertical Percentage is calculated based on column totals, ranking by Value and Vertical Percentage yield exactly the same order. Therefore, only 'Value', 'Horizontal Percentage', and 'Indice' options are shown.

Setting: Ranking order Options: Greater is first, Lesser is first Default: Greater is first Determines what's considered "best" (rank #1). Greater is first: Highest values get rank 1 (sales, satisfaction, etc.) Lesser is first: Lowest values get rank 1 (costs, errors, etc.)

Setting: Ranking scope Options: Global, Per Column, Per Row Default: Global Determines how-to rank the cells. Global: Ranks all cells in the table together Per Column: Ranks cells within each column separately Per Row: Ranks cells within each row separately Examples: Ranking per column: See level of column setting below to choose which column level to consider for Global and Per Row ranking.

Setting: Level of column Options: From 0 to N (N = number of column levels - 1) Default: 1 When using "Global" or "Per Row" ranking scope, choose which column level to consider for ranking. Level 0: Total of all columns (global or per-row) Level 1: First level of columns - global Level 1: First level of columns - per row Level N: Nth level of columns - global Level N: Nth level of columns - per row

documents.t: Setting: Ranking display Options: Add a rank # label within cell Color from Red to Blue Color from Red to Green Custom color gradient Default: Add a rank # label Rank Label​ Shows a numbered badge (1, 2, 3...) in cells. Choose the shape: Shape Options: Circle: Round badge Square: Square badge Rounded Square: Square with rounded corners Example: Color Gradients​ Red to Blue: Red = lowest rank Blue = highest rank Good for neutral comparisons Red to Green: Red = low/bad Green = high/good Commonly understood for positive/negative Custom Color Gradient: Define your own start and end colors Full control over color scheme
When using color display, configure these additional options:

Setting: Color strength Type: Slider (1-10) Default: 7 Controls how saturated/intense the ranking colors are. 1-3: Subtle colors, barely noticeable 4-7: Standard intensity 8-10: Bold, highly visible colors

Setting: Use value for color Type: Toggle Default: Off Normally, colors are based on rank position (rank 1, 2, 3...). Enable this to base colors on actual cell values instead. Example: Without this option: - Rank 1 (value 95%) = Dark green - Rank 2 (value 94%) = Light green - Rank 3 (value 50%) = Light red ← Same color! With this option: - Value 95% = Dark green - Value 94% = Light green - Value 50% = Dark red ← Different color

Setting: Auto font color Type: Toggle Default: Off Automatically adjust text color (black/white) based on background color for better readability. Useful for: Color-based gradients to ensure text is always readable
Exclude certain values from being colored/ranked, useful for "neutral" zones.
Setting: Prevent middle range from coloring Type: Toggle Default: Off When enabled, values between two thresholds are left uncolored.
When "Prevent middle range" is enabled: Exclude From (Start value) Exclude To (End value) Values in this range remain neutral (no color or styling). Example:
Available with the "Custom color gradient" display option.
Type: Color picker Default: White The color for lowest-ranked values.
Type: Color picker Default: Black The color for highest-ranked values.

Configuration: - Enable Ranking: Yes - Ranking Order: Greater is first - Display Format: Color from Red to Green - Color Strength: 8 Result: Top-selling regions show in green, lower performers in red within each column

Configuration: - Enable Ranking: Yes - Ranking Order: Lesser is first (lower costs = better) - Display Format: Add rank # label - Shape: Circle Result: Cost leaders show as [1], [2], [3] within each category

Configuration: - Enable Ranking: Yes - Display Format: Color from Red to Green - Prevent middle range: Yes - Exclude from: 45 - Exclude to: 55 Result: Scores below 45% = red (poor) 45-55% = neutral (no color) Above 55% = green (good)

Configuration: - Enable Ranking: Yes - Display Format: Custom color gradient - Color From: #FF9999 (light brand red) - Color To: #99FF99 (light brand green) Result: Table ranks with custom brand colors

Choose Appropriate Order: "Greater is first" for positive metrics, "Lesser is first" for costs/errors Keep It Simple: Use ranks OR colors, not both simultaneously Color Strength: Use 7-8 for reports, 5-6 for dense data tables Font Color: Enable auto font color with strong gradients Neutral Zones: Use exclude range for naturally neutral metrics (satisfaction 40-60% might be "neutral") Test Accessibility: Ensure colors are distinguishable for color-blind readers

Q: Rankings show but colors aren't appearing A: Check that you've selected a color display option (not "rank label") Q: Color gradient goes the wrong direction A: Verify "Ranking Order" matches your expectations (Greater/Lesser) Q: Rank numbers are hard to read A: Enable "Auto Font Color" or adjust colors in formatting Q: Values seem to rank incorrectly A: Check that "Cell value" property matches your intention (Value, %, Indice) For more help, see the Quick Start Guide.

Every level of the Column Headers and Row Headers editors (⚙, in the Table Headers card) has a Sample across items property. It tells the visual how to build the base of a total or sub-total from the bases of the items it groups (the brands of a year, the modalities of a question…). It replaces the former global "Multiple answer?" and "Rows are repeated items" toggles: the nature of the sample is now declared where it belongs, per level, with no limit on the number of levels. Value Short rule Setup Disjoint (default) Bases add up Nothing to do Shared Bases do not add up: the total keeps the base of one item One switch Native The base comes from your measure, evaluated in the sub-total context A dedicated DAX measure The property sits on the level whose items are combined. With columns Year > Brand, set it on the Brand level to control the Year sub-total, and on the Year level to control the row total across years. On rows, only the last level (leaf rows) is read; the ancestor row levels split the table into independent sub-tables, so setting it there has no effect. note The property is always visible in the editor, even if the level's header label is hidden.

The simplest mode, and the right one for single-answer variables: each respondent falls in exactly one item (Gender, Age bracket, Country…). The groups are distinct sub-populations, so the base of a total is the sum of the bases of its items. Nothing else to set up.

Same as Disjoint, with one rule: do not cumulate the bases. Use it for multiple-answer variables and for batteries of items rated by the same people (a respondent names every brand they know). The items can score differently but their bases are identical, so: the base of the total is the base of one item (the largest), its value is the average count across the items, so value / base stays the cumulated percentage, the horizontal percentage of the children is still computed on the sum of their values (share of citations), the significance tests stop comparing a cell with a "rest of the sample" inflated by the sum of the bases. Shared is exact when every respondent is asked every item. It is only a lower bound of the real base when the items were shown to partly overlapping subsets of the sample. Comparisons between two cells remain treated as independent samples (no covariance is modeled), which makes the tests conservative.

The complex case. The visual stops computing the base of a sub-total and reads the value that Power BI returns for your measure in the sub-total context (the native sub-total API). Base, unweighted base and value of the sub-total are all read from the measure. Use it when not every item is shown to every respondent: for example one quarter of the sample sees the first 10 of 30 items, 60 % see the first 20 and 15 % see the last 20. From the aggregated bases of the items, nobody can tell how many respondents the groups have in common, so neither the sum (too large) nor the largest base (too small) is the true base of the sub-total. Only a measure computed on respondent-level data can give it. The measure must count each respondent once in the sub-total context. With one table row per respondent × item, a plain SUM counts a respondent once per item at the sub-total: -- Wrong at sub-totals: a respondent shown 16 brands is counted 16 times Weight_Base = SUM ( 'Fact'[Weight] ) -- Right: one weight per respondent, whatever the number of items in the filter context Weight_Base = SUMX ( SUMMARIZE ( 'Fact', 'Fact'[Country], 'Fact'[Year], 'Fact'[Wave], 'Fact'[RespondentId] ), CALCULATE ( MAX ( 'Fact'[Weight] ) ) ) On an item cell it returns the base of that item (the filter keeps the respondents shown the item). On a sub-total it returns the real union of respondents exposed to at least one item.

Check the measure first in a native Power BI table: its sub-total row must show the expected union (not Σ of the items). Turn the sub-totals on for the matrix (they are the source of the native values). Put the base measure in the base series; if the displayed values and the unweighted base also need a sub-total context, give them a measure written the same way. Set Native on the level that groups the items.

Where Power BI returns no sub-total (sub-totals off, BLANK), the visual falls back to the Disjoint sum. Native applies to column groups and the total of a row. On the rows axis it behaves as Disjoint (no row sub-total is read). The horizontal percentage of the children stays computed on the sum of their values (share of citations); only the node's own value and bases are native. Significance tests against the rest of the row ("Item vs Other Question Item"): a native sub-total gives the union of a group, never "the group minus this cell", so it cannot supply the base of the complement. Native therefore uses the Shared rule for that complement: the base of the rest is the largest base among the other items, not their sum (which would be roughly 45,000 − 2,500 instead of about 2,500). It is a lower bound of the true base, which makes the test conservative. There is no separate setting for it: Native exists precisely because the items overlap, so summing their bases is never right. Check the base actually used with the Compared base line of the tooltip. Mean tables already use the native sub-total wherever Power BI supplies one, whatever the property: Native matters for percentage tables. A filtered base measure can desynchronize native sub-totals — see Understanding Bases → pitfall.

On weighted data the precision of a proportion depends on the effective base (raw N × design effect E, with E = (Σ weights)² / (N × Σ weights²)), not on the weighted base. To use it in the tests: Provide a measure that returns the effective base and map it to Effective base series in the % series usage card. Choose Separate (effective base) as the variance method in Significance Testing. The effective base is used as the denominator of each group's variance; P1 and P2 still come from the values and base series. Cells without an effective base fall back to their raw base.

Situation Value Single-answer question, demographics Disjoint Multiple-answer question, battery of items asked to everyone Shared Items asked to partly overlapping subsets, you can write a respondent-level measure Native See also Understanding Bases, Percentage Series and Totals & Subtotals.

The Socio Data Management Power BI cross table tool lets you identify statistically significant differences between groups in your data in several manner, depending on your configuration. All feattures includes: Three independent significance tests per table Multiple test types (All columns, Item vs other, Item vs total, Regex, Previous visible column, Previous row) Various display options (icon, font color, background color, border color) Configurable confidence levels (90%, 95%, 99%) Configurable variance methods for percentage tables (pooled, separate, separate with an effective base) Bases that respect your sample design through the per-level Sample across items property
Setting: Significance 1 Options: None, All columns, Item vs other question item, Item versus Total (Base), Regular expression, Previous visible column, Previous row Default: None
Setting: Significance 2 Options: Same as above Default: None

Setting: Significance 3 Options: Same as above Default: None Each test compares different aspects of your data. The three tests are fully independent — each has its own type, display option, regex, and custom icons — and they are not mutually exclusive: several tests can point at the same cell, and you are free to give two or three of them the same symbol (see Combining tests with the same symbol).

Compares each column against all others in the table. You are limited to 156 unique symbols for marking significance. Here is a list of the 156 symbols: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzαβγδεζηθικλμνξοπρστυφχψωΓΔΘΛΞΠΣΦΨΩ🅰🅱🅲🅳🅴🅵🅶🅷🅸🅹🅺🅻🅼🅽🅾🅿🆀🆁🆂🆃🆄🆅🆆🆇🆈🆉ⓐⓑⓒⓓⓔⓕⓖⓗⓘⓙⓚⓛⓜⓝⓞⓟⓠⓡⓢⓣⓤⓥⓦⓧⓨⓩ Use Case: Determine which regions have significantly different satisfaction scores Example: Note that when you have more than one level of column, the significance markers will appear differently per level to avoid confusion.

Compares one response option against all others. important This test is the most used for survey data analysis. You should always prefer this test vs 'Against Total' when comparing response options. Use Case: Highlight if one product preference is significantly different Example:

Compares each item to the overall average at the same level. warning This test has been implemented for legacy purpose and is not generally recommended for any analysis. The reason is that observation (population) of the tested values should always be independent. In this test the observations of each cell is included in the total so it does not ensure this independency rule. Unless you have a good reason, prefer the 'Item vs Other Question Item' test instead.

Uses a regex pattern to identify columns to compare. This option is extremely useful when you are focusing on a brand, a population or a product and want to know which "competitors" are significantly lower or higher. Example 1: You want to compare the age group "50-70 years" against all other age groups in a satisfaction survey. In this example, we have two levels of columns but the regex matches only one item on the first level (50-70): The regex pattern used here is 50-70 which matches partially the column with label "50-70 years". Example 2: You want to compare respondents who answered "yes, once or twice" against all other response options in a survey question split by age groups. In this second example, we match on level two, "yes, once" ich matches columns "Yes, once or twice" under each age group: In this case, only every columns compares to this matched column in each subgroup: Regex level​ Setting: Regex level Options: Same Level, Level 1, Level 2 Default: Same Level Controls on which column depth the regex looks for the reference and how the comparison cascades through the column hierarchy. Same Level (default — historical behavior) The regex is matched anywhere in the column hierarchy and the reference column is compared with its direct siblings (cells sharing the same parent). No comparison is propagated to deeper aggregations. Level 1 The regex must match at the first column level. For every cell at any deeper aggregation, the reference is the cell sharing the same coordinates except for the level‑1 dimension, where the value matches the regex. Level 2 Same logic, but the regex is anchored at the second column level. Levels 1 and 2 are the first two column levels; deeper levels are reached by the cascade. With more than three column levels, use Same Level or anchor the regex on one of the first two levels. Example: with columns Year > Country > Brand and the regex 2024 at Level 1, the test produces: Compared cell Reference (regex-matched) 2025 aggregate 2024 aggregate 2025 / FR aggregate 2024 / FR aggregate 2025 / FR / Renault leaf 2024 / FR / Renault leaf 2026 / UK / Peugeot leaf 2024 / UK / Peugeot leaf … … The reference branch (2024) itself is never flagged. A read‑only Regex match status field is displayed under the regex input. It shows the column paths actually matched by the current regex (or a sample of available column titles when nothing matches), making it easy to diagnose a regex that does not produce the expected highlights.

Compares each column to the nearest visible column before it, at the same depth in the column hierarchy — skipping over any columns hidden by a Mask Pattern. Use Case: Track a single brand's evolution year over year, or any period-over-period comparison, without cluttering the table with every other response option. This test is what makes a "previous period" comparison work even when you have hidden most of the columns. For example, with columns Year > Brand and a mask that keeps only MyBrand visible under each year (NOT BrandName = "MyBrand"), each year effectively shows a single leaf column. This test aligns each one with the previous visible leaf column — 2022 vs. 2021, 2023 vs. 2022, and so on — even though 2022 / MyBrand and 2021 / MyBrand don't share the same immediate parent column-wise; they're simply the two closest visible leaves in table order. note The very first visible column at a given depth has no previous visible column to compare against, so it is never marked significant by this test. tip This test runs at every level of the column hierarchy independently, not just the leaves. If your top-level columns (e.g. the years themselves) aren't masked, you'll also get a year-over-year comparison at that level, in addition to the leaf-level one.

Compares each row to the previous row in the table, in the same column — a row-over-row equivalent of Previous visible column, useful when your rows are an ordered sequence (a scale, a ranking, consecutive periods represented as rows instead of columns). Use Case: Flag which item in an ordered list of rated items jumps significantly compared to the one just above it. Unlike All Columns (which uses each column's own total as the sample size), this test uses each row's own base — consistent with a last row level declared Shared in Sample Across Items, where every row is an item with its own respondent base. Filtered base measures can silently break significance If your base measure is a filtered SUM (e.g. filtered to hide structurally-blank rows), the base feeding these tests can desynchronize from what's actually displayed — see Understanding Bases → filtered base measure pitfall. note Native Power BI subtotal rows are automatically skipped — both as a row being tested and as a candidate "previous row" — so a subtotal never gets compared, and the row right after it compares against the last real data row above the subtotal, not the subtotal itself. note The first row in the table (or the first row after any leading subtotal) has no previous row to compare against, so it is never marked significant by this test.

Setting: Significance level Options: 90%, 95%, 99% Default: 95% The confidence threshold for determining significance. 90%: More lenient (flags more differences) 95%: Standard business level 99%: Strict scientific standard info You usually do not change this settings. Choose a higher level (99%) for critical decisions. See the number behind the marker The pass/fail marker only tells you whether a cell crossed this threshold. To see the actual, continuous confidence level for every cell — independent of this setting — enable Significance confidence level in the Cell Tooltip.

Setting: Signif. Var. Method Options: Pooled proportion, Separate, Separate (effective base) Default: Pooled How variance is calculated when comparing percentages. Pooled: Treats all groups as one population (more conservative) Separate: Treats groups separately (more sensitive to differences) Separate (effective base): Same as Separate, but each group's variance uses a ready-made effective base read from the Effective base series instead of the raw base: t = (P1 − P2) / √(P1(1−P1)/EffBase1 + P2(1−P2)/EffBase2). Use it for weighted samples, where the effective base (raw N × design effect) is smaller than N. P1 and P2 still come from the values and base series; when a cell has no effective base, its raw base is used. tip In usual situation, leave the default to Pooled proportion. Choose Separate proportion option when group sizes differ greatly.

Setting: Significance view option Options: Icon, Font Color, Background Color, Cell border Color Default: Icon How significant values are marked: Icon: Small symbol/marker appears in cell (Red for significantly lower, Green for significantly higher) Custom Icon Images You can replace the default green/red SVG triangles with your own images. When the view option is set to Icon, two additional fields appear in the significance settings: Custom icon positive (base64): Paste a base64 data URI (data:image/png;base64,…) to use a custom image for positive significance. Custom icon negative (base64): Paste a base64 data URI for negative significance. Leave either field empty to keep the default SVG triangle for that direction. Custom images are displayed at 12 × 12 px, vertically centered in the cell. Font Color: Text color changes red or green to highlight significance Background Color: Cell background changes red or green to highlight significance Option for backGround color When you choose background color, you can also choose to apply a gradient custom colors instead of a solid color. Choosing this option will make a new option appear to solect the gradient colors and the orientation of gradient. Border Color: Cell border changes red or green to highlight significance

The Legend sub-card (inside Significance Settings) adds an automatic legend below the table that explains the significance markers to report readers. Enable it with the Show legend toggle at the top of the sub-card.

The legend automatically adapts its content to match the display mode(s) actively used by your significance test(s): Background / Border mode​ When at least one significance test uses Background or Border display, the legend shows three colored squares with editable labels: A square in the neutral cell background color → label defaults to "Not significantly different" A square in the positive significance color → label defaults to "Significantly higher" A square in the negative significance color → label defaults to "Significantly lower" All three labels support the fx button (DAX measure binding) for dynamic, filter-context-sensitive text. Icon mode​ When at least one significance test uses Icon display, the legend shows the actual icons (custom image or default SVG triangles) beside an editable text label for each active significance test (Signif 1 label, Signif 2 label, Signif 3 label). A matching Signif n label suffix field lets you append a dynamic value (via the fx button) without creating a dedicated DAX measure for the full text — the program concatenates the two parts with a space. Font Color mode​ When at least one significance test uses Font Color display, the legend renders "123/123" in green (positive) and red (negative) beside an editable text label for each active significance test. The same suffix fields apply.
Active significance tests Legend layout 1 test active Centered below the table 2 or 3 tests active Blocks spread across the row (first left-aligned, last right-aligned, others distributed between)
All legend text shares a single FontControl (font family, bold, italic, underline, size) configurable in the Legend sub-card.

Setting Description Default Neutral label Label for the neutral color square (background/border mode) "Not significantly different" Positive label Label for the positive color square (background/border mode) "Significantly higher" Negative label Label for the negative color square (background/border mode) "Significantly lower" Signif 1 label Text label for significance 1 (icon / font color mode) (empty) Signif 1 label suffix Dynamic suffix appended after the Signif 1 label (empty) Signif 2 label Text label for significance 2 (icon / font color mode) (empty) Signif 2 label suffix Dynamic suffix appended after the Signif 2 label (empty) Signif 3 label Text label for significance 3 (icon / font color mode) (empty) Signif 3 label suffix Dynamic suffix appended after the Signif 3 label (empty) All label fields support the fx button for DAX measure binding, allowing the legend text to update dynamically based on filter context. :::tip Composing dynamic labels without extra measures The suffix fields are designed for cases where the label has a fixed prefix and a dynamic part. For example, set Signif 1 label to "Significantly different from" (constant) and bind Signif 1 label suffix to a DAX measure that returns the currently selected reference value. The visual concatenates them with a space — no need to create a dedicated measure just to produce the full sentence. :::
You can configure up to three tests, each independently: Different display methods for each test Different test types simultaneously Regex patterns for flexible comparison

The tests are not mutually exclusive. Because each test writes its own result on every cell, you can point several tests at the same cell and, if you wish, mark them with the same symbol (same view option and, for icons, the same custom image). This is what lets you express an OR relationship. For example, to flag every cell that is significantly different from column A or column B, set up two Regular expression tests — one matching A, the other matching B — and give both the same icon. A cell that is significant against either reference then carries that single symbol. note When two or three tests resolve to the same icon on the same cell, the icon is drawn once (the union is not duplicated). Font-color, background and border modes stack as CSS classes, so keep those on distinct tests if you want to tell them apart.
documents.s: Combining tests with the same symbol

documents.t: Tests such as Item vs other question item compare a cell with the complement of its group. For a battery of items answered by the same respondents, summing the other items' bases inflates that complement. Declare such levels Shared (or Native) in the header editors so the complement is built correctly — see Sample Across Items.
documents.s: Sample design and the "rest of the sample"

documents.t: Hides the first variable in comparative displays for cleaner visuals (see masking in table-content).
For percentage tables: Chi-square test of independence For mean tables: T-tests or ANOVA (depending on number of groups)
A cell marked as significant means: The difference between groups is unlikely due to chance At the chosen confidence level Given the sample sizes

Significance depends on sample size (large samples show more differences) Practical significance ≠ statistical significance (a 1% difference might be statistically significant but not practically important) Always consider context, not just statistics
Significance tests require special data series:

Significance Series: The counts/values used for testing Base Series: The total base for calculating proportions Which percentage is tested? By default the proportion tested is the vertical percentage, with the column total as sample size. When Cell Percentage is turned on, it replaces the vertical percentage in every test type: the proportion tested is the cell's value divided by its own base, and the sample size is that cell's own base. The same data can therefore give a different verdict depending on which percentage is selected.

Mean Series: The mean values to test Standard Deviation Series: Measure of variability Count Series: Sample size Configure these in data settings under: "Significance Series" (percentage tables) "Mean Series for Significance" (mean tables)

Choose Appropriate Test: Match test type to your question (all columns vs vs-total) Clear Display: Use one view option per test for clarity Document Level: Note which significance level you're using in reports Consider Sample Size: Small sample sizes can miss real differences Practical Significance: Don't rely solely on statistics; consider business context

Q: Significance markers don't appear A: Ensure you've configured significance series in data settings Q: All cells are marked significant A: Your significance level might be too lenient (90%); try 99% Q: No cells marked significant A: Check sample sizes; very small groups won't show significance For more help, see the Quick Start Guide or contact support.
Customize how rows and columns are arranged in your table with flexible sorting options.

Setting: Row sorting Options: None, Row Label (Alphabetical), Column Value Default: None When different from 'None', rows are sorted depending on the different settings. Otherwise, rows remain in the order they come from the data source. See About sorting elements in Power BI section for more details. None​ Rows appear in the order they come from the data source. Row Label (Alphabetical)​ Sorts rows alphabetically by their label. Example: Before: North, South, East, West After: East, North, South, West caution If you use this setting for numeric labels like "1", "2", "3", the '10' label will be considered as coming before "2" in alphabetical order (1,10,2,3,4...). In such cases, consider using 'Last Row/Column Positioning' to fix specific label ("10") at the end or use the new "find number in row labels" feature. Column Value​ Sorts rows based on the values found in one specific column of the table, which you designate with a column path. Use Cases: Sort products by highest sales Rank regions by satisfaction score Order responses by frequency Writing the column path​ Setting: Row Sort on column (visible only when Row Sorting = Column Value) Type: Text input Format: One column label per hierarchy level, separated by a pipe | The path walks the column hierarchy from left to right: the first segment is a label of the first (top) column level, the second segment a label of the second level, and so on, until it reaches the column whose values must drive the sort. Example with two column levels — a table crossed by Gender > Age: Male Female 18-34 35-54 18-34 35-54 Product A 12 18 25 31 Product B 34 22 17 28 Product C 21 40 39 14 To sort the rows on... Enter this path the Female / 35-54 column Female|35-54 the Male / 18-34 column Male|18-34 the Female subtotal (whole group) Female the grand Total column (leave empty) With the path Female|35-54 and a Descending order, the rows of the example above are reordered on that single column: Product A (31), Product B (28), Product C (14). Path rules​ Rule Detail Separator The pipe character |. One segment per column level, top level first. Case & spaces Ignored. female | 35-54 is the same as Female|35-54. Matching The exact displayed header label, matched in full. This is not a regex and not a partial match (unlike the pattern used by Significance). Quotes Optional. "Female"|"35-54" is equivalent to Female|35-54. Empty path Sorts on the row Total column. Partial path Fewer segments than there are levels targets the subtotal of that column group (Female on a 2-level table = the Female subtotal). Number of levels Any depth is supported — a 3-level table accepts 2025|France|My Brand. :::tip Finding the exact paths of your table The Regex match status read-only field of the Significance card lists all the column paths that actually exist in your table. It displays them with a > separator (Female > 35-54), so replace > with | before pasting a path into the sort field. ::: caution If the path matches no column, no error is displayed: every row gets a null sort value and the rows simply stay in their original order. Check the spelling of each segment, and remember that the labels are the ones displayed in the table (after any renaming or masking). Rows that have no value in the designated column are always pushed to the end of the table, whatever the sorting order. info The Column Property setting (Value / Horizontal Percentage / Indice) decides which number of the designated cell is used. For instance Female|35-54 combined with Horizontal Percentage sorts the rows on the horizontal percentage of that cell.

Setting: Find number in Row Labels Options: True, False Default: False When enabled, this setting extracts numeric values from row labels for sorting purposes. This is particularly useful when your row labels contain numbers mixed with text. Example: Text sorting Find in number sorting Brand A (2024) Brand A (2024) Brand A (2025) Brand B (2024) Brand B (2024) Brand C (2024) Brand B (2025) Brand A (2025) Brand C (2024) Brand B (2025) Brand C (2025) Brand C (2025) Example with purely numeric labels: Text sorting Find in number sorting 1 1 10 2 2 3 3 4 ... ... 9 10 Example with ranges in labels: Text sorting Find in number sorting none from 1 to 50 beyond 100 from 50 to 100 from 1 to 50 beyond 100 from 50 to 100 none tip This setting is particularly useful for sorting labels that include years, ages, or other numeric indicators within text. Only the first number found in the label is considered for sorting. If the number is prefixed with a minus sign (e.g., "-5"), it will be treated as a negative number.

Setting: Row sorting order Options: Ascending, Descending Default: Ascending Controls whether sorted values go low-to-high or high-to-low. Example (Column Value sorting): Ascending: Smallest values first (1, 2, 3...) Descending: Largest values first (...100, 99, 98) Example (Raw label sorting): Ascending: Alphabetical order (A, B, C...) Descending: Reverse alphabetical order (Z, Y, X...)

Setting: Column property Options: Value, Horizontal Percentage, Cell Percentage, Indice Default: Value When using "Column Value" sort, choose which metric to sort by. Value: Value of cells (AND Vertical Percentage) Horizontal Percentage: Percentage within row Cell Percentage: Value divided by the cell's own base (see Cell Percentage). Unlike the vertical percentage, it can give a different order from Value when bases vary from row to row. Indice: Index value tip For percentage tables, sorting by "Value" and "Vertical Percentage" yield exactly the same order, reason why only 'value', 'horizontal percentage' and 'Indice' options are shown.

Force certain rows or columns to stay at the beginning or end, regardless of sort order. info In the folowing settings, multiple labels can be specified separated by commas. The comparison is not case sensitive and enclose labels in double quotes if they contain comma. e.g., My Brand, My First Competitor or "Not Answered","no, never"

Setting: 'First row(s)' label(s) Type: Text input Format: Comma-separated Example: My Brand, My First Competitor These rows always appear first in your table, even if a sort would normally place them elsewhere.

Setting: 'Last row(s)' label(s) Type: Text input Format: Comma-separated Example: Not Answered, Other These rows always appear last in your table. Example: Configuration: Last rows = "Not Answered","Other" Result table: - Product A - Product B - Product C - Not Answered (always last) - Other (always last)

Setting: Column sort on labels Type: True/False Example: False When enabled, columns are sorted depending on their labels alphabetically. Otherwise, columns remain in the order they come from the data source. See About sorting elements in Power BI section for more details.

Setting: Find number in Column Labels Options: True, False Default: False When enabled, this setting extracts numeric values from column labels for sorting purposes. This is particularly useful when your column labels contain numbers mixed with text. This feature works the same as for row labels. See Find number in Row Labels section for more details.
Setting: 'First column(s)' label(s) Type: Text input Format: Comma-separated Example: Current Year, Last Year These columns always appear first.
Setting: 'Last column(s)' label(s) Type: Text input Format: Comma-separated Example: Previous Year, Two Years Ago These columns always appear last.

Power BI has its own sorting behavior that can interact with SDM Power BI Table's sorting settings. Here are some key points to understand: Power BI will use either a logic alphabetical order for rows and columns, either the order it find data in the data source. This depends on the data model and how fields are configured. There is a way to create a custom sort order in Power BI by creating a separate "sort order" column in your data model and linking it to the field you want to sort. This will naturally send the data in this order to the SDM Power BI Table visual and therefore will not require any sorting setting in the visual itself. Socio Data Management © propose custom service to help you create automatically such sort columns in your data model if needed from any datasource (SPSS, CSV, Excel, SQL, Triple-S XML etc...). These sort columns are automatically attached to the relevant fields in the data model so that ALL Power BI visuals (including SDM Power BI Table) will use them for sorting. Even if you use the sort settings in the data source, any sorting settings in the SDM Power BI Table visual will override Power BI's sorting. Unless you use either the sort columns trick or the SDM Power BI Table visual sorting settings, there is no guarantee about the order of rows and columns in Power BI, as it can depend on various factors like data refreshes, model changes, etc.
documents.s: About sorting elements in Power BI

documents.t: Use Column Sort for Insights: Sort by the most important metric (sales, satisfaction, etc.) Use first rows/columns for Key Items: like your brand or your main topic of research Use last rows/columns for "Other", "Not answered", undefined or "Missing categories: Keeps focus on main data Totals and subTotals columns are Allways fixed before the detailed columns Alphabetical for Stability: Use alphabetical sort for consistent report appearance Limit Fixed Items: Too many fixed rows makes the table confusing Consider User Expectations: Sort in a logical order for your audience

Multiple Sort Levels: Combine with ranking to show top performers visually Dynamic Sorting: Power BI's interactions allow end-users to click columns to resort (with Power BI native features) Regional Reports: Use First/Last columns to keep comparison columns visible while scrolling

Q: Sort doesn't seem to work A: Ensure you've selected a sort method other than "None" Q: My first/last rows aren't appearing A: Check the exact spelling and case of row labels Q: Column value sort uses wrong column A: Verify you selected the correct column in "Row Sort Column" setting Q: I set "Column Value" sorting but nothing moves A: The column path matched no column, so all rows share a null sort value. Check every segment of the path against the labels displayed in the table, and make sure the segments are separated by a pipe | (not by >, which is only the display format of the Regex match status field). For more help, see the Quick Start Guide.
The Table Contents section controls what data is displayed in your table and how it's aggregated.
Setting: Table type (Percentage or Mean) Default: Percentage

Used to analyze distributions, proportions, and response rates. Available Displays: Values: Raw count or sum Vertical Percentage (%): Percentage within each column Horizontal Percentage (%): Percentage within each row Cell Percentage (%): Each cell's value divided by its own base (alternative to the vertical percentage) Indice: Index value (typically 100 = average) Example: In a survey of 100 respondents: Very Satisfied Satisfied Neutral North 45 (60%) 30 (40%) 25 (33%) South 35 (47%) 45 (60%) 45 (60%) Total 80 (53%) 75 (50%) 70 (47%)

Used to analyze averages and their statistical properties. Available Displays: Mean Values: Average of the metric Count: Number of observations used in calculation Standard Deviation: Measure of variability Indice: Index based on mean values Example: Average customer satisfaction score:
Label: Show values Type: Toggle Default: Off When enabled, displays the raw count or sum in each cell.
Label: Vertical percentage Type: Toggle Default: On Shows each cell's value as a percentage of its column total. Useful for comparing across categories within groups.
Label: Horizontal percentage Type: Toggle Default: Off Shows each cell's value as a percentage of its row total. Useful for comparing category distribution within segments.

Label: Cell percentage Type: Toggle Default: Off Shows each cell's value divided by its own base, read directly from the Base Series at that crossing: Cell Percentage = Value (row × column) / Base (row × column) How it differs from the vertical percentage: the vertical percentage divides by the column total of the Base Series, which the visual builds by going through the rows. Cell Percentage only looks at the current crossing. Use it when your model already provides the right denominator for every cell, for example a base that varies from one row to the next (items asked to different sub-samples, a rating scale with a per-item base, a "value + its base" pair computed in DAX). Example: Value Base (per cell) Cell % Brand A / North 120 300 40% Brand B / North 90 150 60% ← asked only to half the sample With the vertical percentage, both rows would be divided by the same column total. Subtotals and totals: on a group row or column, value and base are both summed over the children, and the ratio of the two sums is shown. No extra setting is needed. Mutually exclusive with Vertical Percentage: both use the same slot in the cell and act as the table's main percentage, so turning one on turns the other off automatically. It replaces the vertical percentage everywhere downstream, not just in the display: Significance tests: the proportion tested is the Cell Percentage, and the sample size is the cell's own base instead of the column total. The same data can therefore give a different verdict depending on which percentage is selected. See Significance Testing. Sorting and ranking: Cell Percentage becomes available as a Column Property and a Ranking cell value. Tooltip: a separate Cell % line can be shown, see Tooltip. Cell rules: available as the cellPct variable, see Cell Rules. Excel export: exported in place of the vertical percentage. note Cell Percentage only applies to percentage tables. It is left empty on mean tables.

Label: Show indice Type: Toggle Default: Off Displays index values (typically with 100 as base). Useful for comparing relative performance against an average. Calculation: (Cell Value / Average) × 100

When the incoming dataset contains no rows — most commonly when a page or report filter excludes everything — the table is never drawn (no empty "shell" made of a column header and a Base row at 0), and the Excel export button is hidden whatever the Show Excel Export Button setting says, since there would be nothing to export. What the visual shows instead — a message you style yourself, or nothing at all — is controlled by the Global Threshold card. That card also hides the table on a test of your own (a base below your publication threshold, say): see Global Threshold. Clear on Empty dataset has been replaced The toggle that used to live here only chose between a hard-coded "No data to display" message and a blank screen. It is gone, replaced by the Global Threshold card — its Empty Panel property has the opposite polarity, and the old value is not carried over. See Coming from Clear on Empty dataset.

WHY USE MASKING WHEN POWER BI CAN FILTER DATA? When you filter data in Power BI, the underlying data is removed from the visual, which can affect calculations like totals and percentages. Masking allows you to hide specific data points while still including them in calculations, ensuring accurate results.

Label: Mask Pattern Type: Text area Default: Empty Allows you to mask (hide) data from specific rows or columns using regular expressions. User will input a pattern to match the rows/columns to be hidden. As an example, if you want to show ONLY Brand A and Brand B, you need to hide everything which is NOT Brand A or B. Label_Brand != BrandA AND Label_Brand != BrandB or better with the IN operator NOT Label_Brand IN (BrandA, BrandB) Therefore, if also you do not want the "No answer" to gender question while still using it in calculations: (NOT Label_Brand IN (BrandA, BrandB)) OR Customer_Gender = "Not Stated" etc ... (NOT Label_Brand IN (BrandA, BrandB)) OR (Customer_Gender IN ("Not Stated", Other)) Beware of the inverted logic of masking. The pattern defines what to HIDE, this can be somewaht counter-intuitive at first. Valid operators are: IN - for multiple values AND - for logical conjunction OR - for logical disjunction NOT - for negation = - Equals != - Not equals < - Less than > - Greater than LIKE - Pattern matching with % wildcard <= and >= does not exist if you want to filter for years greater than or equal to 2020, you need to use Year > 2019 The LIKE operator works with the % symbol, for example: Customer_Gender LIKE %ale Will hide M'ale' AND Fem'ale', and therefore show only "Not Stated" and "Other" To show only Male AND Female, you need to invert the logic: NOT Customer_Gender LIKE %ale Will show ONLY Male and Female Blank / empty values If a category has no value in your data (Power BI shows it as blank), it appears as an empty label in the table — not the word "Null". A pattern like Label_Brand = Null will therefore never match it. To target blank values specifically, compare against an empty string: Label_Brand = "" To exclude blanks while keeping everything else, use the greater-than operator: Label_Brand > "" Use Cases: Hide sensitive data in shared reports Remove small brands/categories from view Focus on top-performing segments Filter out "Other" or "Not answered" categories while still taking them into account for calculations
For detailed series configuration options (Value Series, Base Series, Mean Series, etc.), see: Percentage Series Usage — For percentage tables Mean Series Usage — For mean tables

Choose Table Type First: Percentage vs Mean fundamentally changes how data is displayed Limit Display Fields: Use 2-3 display options maximum for clarity Use Masking Sparingly: Masked data is still calculated but hidden Precision for Business: Use 0-1 decimal places for most business reporting Totals Context: Show totals to help readers understand the base size
Totals Settings — Configure total rows and columns Series Configuration — Detailed data mapping Sorting Options — Arrange rows and columns

Q: Values appear as "0%" or very small numbers A: Check that your base series is correctly mapped in percentage series settings. Q: Indice values don't look right A: Ensure you've configured both values and base series correctly. Q: Mask pattern isn't working A: Check your regular expression syntax. Use simple patterns like Total before complex regex. For more help, see the Quick Start Guide.

Table Headers controls how column and row header levels look and are laid out — background, font, an optional logo, title cut, sub-total columns, column width and row height, gaps between groups, column separators, the sample type of the level's items, and (for row headers) the layout of each level. It is driven by two schema-driven editors — Column Headers and Row Headers — each managing an open-ended list of per-level blocks, one block per hierarchy level, with no cap on the number of levels. Replaces the fixed, level-capped settings of CrossTable CrossTable uses fixed, level-suffixed settings (Column Logo Lv1/Lv2/Lv3 and Row Logo Lv1/Lv2 data roles, Top-Level / Sub-Level Column Header and Row header format cards, Show Level 1/2 Sub-Total, Multiple answer, Rows are repeated items). SDM Xtended Table has none of them: everything that depends on a header level is a field of that level's block in the ⚙ editors described below. The Cell format card (Custom Element Formatting) is unchanged. Want to bind logos from a DAX measure? See the Header Logos tutorial for a full, click-by-click walkthrough — from base64-encoding your images to wiring a CONCATENATEX measure into the Header logos lookup. Location: Format pane → Table Headers card, holding two JSON text fields (Column headers, Row headers) managed through their own ⚙ gear icons, plus a Header logos field with its own icon. The icons appear at the top-right of the visual in the report's Edit view.

Click the Column editor icon or the Row editor icon to open the editor. Each shows one block per header level and an Add level button: Editor Levels Cap Column Headers One block per column-header depth (Level 1 = outermost) None — add as many levels as your column hierarchy has. Row Headers One block per row depth, outermost first; the last level is the row labels themselves (the leaf rows) None — add as many levels as your row hierarchy has. Within a block, the fields are grouped in three collapsible sections: Header (open by default: colors, font, logo, additional CSS and, for columns, the title cut), Sub-total (the sub-total column style and the Sample across items property) and Layout (size, gap before each group, separator, row layout). The Show this header switch stays outside the sections, always visible. A level with no block configured simply shows the active style theme's default — you only need to add a level to override something. 📸 Screenshot — Format pane / editor dialog tableheaders-editor-open.png — the Column Headers (or Row Headers) ⚙ editor open, showing one configured level block with its fields.
documents.s: The ⚙ editors — Column Headers / Row Headers

documents.t: Field Applies to Type Default Description Show this header Columns, Rows Toggle On Unchecking it hides this level's header row (columns) or column / banner (rows) — see Hiding a header level below. The styling fields of this level are hidden in the editor while it's off, since there's nothing left to style. Header colors Columns, Rows Inherit from theme / Custom Inherit from theme Inherit lets the style theme decide this level's background and font color — the recommended default when you're only adding a level for its logo. Custom reveals Background and Font color below. Background Columns, Rows Color White (Custom only) Background of every header cell at this level — including the corner cell, for Column level 1. Font color Columns, Rows Color Black (Custom only) Text color at this level. Font Columns, Rows Font family — Typography for this level. Font size Columns, Rows 6–40 11 Bold / Italic / Underline Columns, Rows Toggle — Logo series Columns, Rows Measure or named logo table (optional) (none) A measure from the Additional Series data role providing a base64 logo for this level, or a named table of the Header logos lookup. See Logos on a header below. Logo placement Columns, Rows Logo only / Logo above text / Logo under text Logo above text How the logo combines with the header label — no effect if no logo resolves for a given header. Logo size (px) Columns, Rows 8–100 24 Logo height at this level. Additional CSS Columns, Rows Free text (multi-line) (empty) Raw CSS declarations appended to this level's generated style rule — see Additional CSS below. Title cut (when horizontal scroll is forbidden) Columns Ellipsis / 2 lines + ellipsis / As many lines as needed Ellipsis How long titles of this level are cut when Forbid horizontal scroll is on — see Title cut. Only shown while the level's header is shown. Width (last level only) Columns Auto / Distribute equally / Minimal / Fixed (px) Auto Width of the data columns — see Size. Height of each group of this level Rows Auto / Distribute equally / Minimal / Fixed (px) Minimal Height of each row (last level) or of each sub-table (outer levels) — see Size. Width / Height (px) Columns, Rows 10–2000 100 (columns) / 30 (rows) Only shown when the size mode is Fixed. Gap before each group (px) Columns, Rows 0–100 0 Space before each group of this level — see Gaps between groups. Row layout Rows Side column / Hierarchical Side column See Row layout below. Show sub-total column Columns Toggle On Shows the sub-total column of this level (the one that sums its sub-columns) — see Sub-total columns. Sub-total colors … Sub-total underline Columns Same as the header fields Inherit from theme Style of this level's sub-total column (header and cells). Only shown while Show sub-total column is on. Column separator Columns None / Dotted / Dashed / Axis / Solid / Double None A vertical line on the left of each group of this level. See Column separators. Separator color / width (px) Columns Color / 1–8 #999999 / 1 Only shown when a separator style is selected. Sample across items Columns, Rows Disjoint / Shared / Native Disjoint How the items of this level relate to each other — see Sample across items. Changes save back into the underlying JSON field (Column headers / Row headers) and persist with the report, like any other formatting property. 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-logoplacement-montage.png — the same header with a logo, compared across the three Logo placement options: Logo only, Logo above text, Logo under text.

To hide a column or row header level, add a level block in the relevant ⚙ editor and uncheck "Show this header" — there's no separate on/off setting elsewhere; this field is the mechanism. A level with no block configured is always shown at its theme default, so hiding one means adding a block for it (via Add level) specifically to turn it off. This is a genuine removal, not a CSS-level hide: the visual doesn't create that header row (columns) or column / banner (rows) at all, rather than rendering it invisibly. That matters because a naive hide (visibility: hidden, which still reserves the space, or display: none on a single row-header cell, which shifts every cell after it out of alignment) gets either wasted whitespace or a misaligned table — neither of which happens here. The corner cell's span shrinks to match whichever levels remain. A hidden column level can still show its sub-total column: the Show sub-total column field stays available even when the header itself is hidden. Row headers: hiding also affects the Base/Unweighted Base/Signif Base row labels On row headers, the label column used by the Base/Unweighted Base/Signif Base total rows is the leaf row-label level — hiding that level hides the label of those total rows too, so they keep the same column count as the data rows above them (a total row can't have one more column than the data rows without breaking alignment). 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-hidelevel-before.png — a table with the redundant header level still shown. 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-hidelevel-after.png — the same table with that level's Show this header unchecked: the level is gone, corner cell span shrunk to match.

Two independent sources can supply a header's logo, tried in this order — the first one that resolves for a given header label wins: Header logos (the lookup editor, below) — a simple label → logo map, resolved entirely inside the visual, at zero query cost. Logo series (the per-level field above) — a measure from the Additional Series data role.

Click the Header Logos icon to open a small editor listing label / logo pairs — type the header's exact displayed label and paste (or bind via a DAX measure and the fx button) its base64 logo. Prefer this over Logo series when the logo only depends on the category A measure bound through Additional Series lives in the Matrix's Values bucket, so Power BI evaluates and transmits it for every cell (row × column) — not once per header. With only a handful of distinct logos (e.g. one flag per country) repeated across thousands of cells, that can by itself push a large table into matrix truncation. The Header logos lookup has none of this cost: it's resolved once, in memory, from a small JSON list. A convenient way to keep this list in sync with a lookup table is a DAX measure that concatenates it into JSON, bound to the Header logos lookup (JSON) field via the fx button so it's recomputed once per report render (respecting slicers) rather than per cell: Header Logos JSON = "[" & CONCATENATEX( VALUES( Country[Label_country] ), "{""label"":""" & Country[Label_country] & """,""logo"":""" & MAX( Country[Logo_Country] ) & """}", "," ) & "]" See the Header Logos tutorial for the full walkthrough, from base64-encoding your images to binding this measure. Named logo tables — more than one lookup in the same field​ By default every entry in Header logos lands in one shared namespace — any level whose label matches gets that logo. If two unrelated sets of logos happen to share a label (or you'd simply rather keep them apart — e.g. country flags at one level and brand marks at another, both produced by the same DAX measure into one JSON array), tag each entry with an optional table field: [ { "label": "France", "logo": "data:image/png;base64,...", "table": "countries" }, { "label": "Brand A", "logo": "data:image/png;base64,...", "table": "brands" } ] Entries with no table field stay in the default (untagged) namespace and keep applying automatically to any level that hasn't opted into a named table — this is fully backward compatible with a plain flat lookup. To make a level use one named table specifically, pick it from that level's Logo series dropdown — named tables found in your Header logos JSON appear there (prefixed 🖼️ Header Logos:), alongside the normal Additional Series measures. A level can use either a named lookup table or a Logo series measure, never both at once — picking one clears the other. 📸 Screenshot — Format pane settings tableheaders-namedtable-dropdown.png — a level's Logo series dropdown open, showing a 🖼️-prefixed named table entry alongside normal Additional Series measures. Renamed or deleted table If a level points at a named table that no longer exists in Header logos (renamed, or its entries removed), that level silently falls back to showing the plain text label — exactly as if no logo were configured — rather than erroring.

Still useful when a logo genuinely needs to be calculated (not a fixed lookup) — pick a measure from the Additional Series data role in the Logo series field of a level. Remember its per-cell evaluation cost on large tables; scan a few rows before assuming a constant value doesn't hold, and prefer Header logos whenever the mapping is really just "one logo per category name". Security Every image field of the visual accepts base64 data URIs only — no external URL is ever fetched. This applies to both the lookup and the Logo series.

With two or more row levels, every outer row level (every level except the last one, which holds the row labels) picks independently how it renders, through its Row layout field: Layout Rendering Side column (default) The level's label is a narrow, row-spanning column on the left, next to the rows it groups. Hierarchical The level's label becomes a full-width banner row above its group of rows, instead of a side column. Side column Hierarchical ┌──────────┬────────┬─────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ │ Trust │ ... │ │ Fundamentals │ │Fundamen- ├────────┼─────┤ ├──────────┬─────┬──────┤ │ tals │ Quality│ ... │ │ Trust │ ... │ │ ├──────────┼────────┼─────┤ ├──────────┼─────┼──────┤ │ Crafted │ Comfort│ ... │ │ Quality │ ... │ │ │ space ├────────┼─────┤ ├──────────────────────┤ │ │ Design │ ... │ │ Crafted space │ └──────────┴────────┴─────┘ ├──────────┬─────┬──────┤ │ Comfort │ ... │ │ └──────────┴─────┴──────┘ Layouts can be mixed across levels — for example Level 1 as a banner and Level 2 as a side column. A banner row picks up its own level's Background / Font / Additional CSS — style it like any other level. Combine it with Additional CSS to get, for example, a dashed border framing each section. The Row layout field has no effect on the last row level (the leaf rows), whose labels are always the row-label column. Combine row layouts with a Gap before each group to add a vertical space between consecutive sub-tables. 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-rowlayout-sidecolumn.png — a 2-level row grouping with Level 1's Row layout set to Side column (the narrow first-column look). 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-rowlayout-hierarchical.png — the same table with Hierarchical: Level 1's label as a full-width banner row above its Level 2 group. Known limits Side-by-side (Table of Tables) mode and freeze panes are not specially handled for banner rows — a banner scrolls normally, and side-by-side mode ignores the Hierarchical setting.
documents.s: Row layout: Side column vs. Hierarchical

documents.t: The Layout section of a level sets the size of what that level lays out. The same four modes exist for columns (Width) and rows (Height of each group of this level): Mode Columns (last level) Rows Auto The browser distributes the width and the table grows to fill the visual width. (Default for columns) The natural heights are stretched so the rows fill the visual height. Distribute equally All data columns get the same width, sharing the available width. All groups of the level get the same height, sharing the available height. Minimal (just what is needed) Each column takes only the width it needs; empty space is left on the right. Each row takes only the height it needs; empty space is left at the bottom. (Default for rows, i.e. the historical behavior.) Fixed (px) Every data column is exactly the given number of pixels wide. Every group is exactly the given number of pixels high. Columns: the setting is read on the last column level (the leaf columns); parent levels are simple spans over them. Rows: each row level can be set independently. On the last level, Height applies to each row; on an outer level it applies to each group of that level (for example each country of a Country > Brand hierarchy), and the inner levels then share the height of their parent's group. This replaces the former Row height (px) Table option. A Fixed height is a target for the whole group, including any gap.

The Gap before each group (px) field adds empty space in front of each group of the level, in standard mode and in Tile mode alike. It replaces the former Row group spacing Table option and the Group gap / Sub-group gap / Row gap Tile-mode settings, and works at any level. Columns: horizontal space before each group of the level (not before the first group of its parent). A column separator of the same level is drawn centered inside that space. The gap is also applied before the level's sub-total column. Rows, outer level: a vertical spacer row before each group of the level, i.e. between two consecutive sub-tables (one country, one wave…). The spacer is a real empty row, not a border, so it doesn't disturb zebra striping or frozen rows. With a single sub-table there is nothing to space. Rows, last level: space between two consecutive leaf rows. 0 (default) means no gap.

When Table options → Forbid horizontal scroll is on, the table is fitted to the width of the visual: a column can no longer widen to fit its title, so titles are cut. The Title cut field of each column level chooses how: Option Rendering Ellipsis (default) One line, ending with "…" 2 lines + ellipsis Up to two lines, ending with "…" if it still doesn't fit As many lines as needed The title wraps on as many lines as necessary The field has no effect while horizontal scroll is allowed.
documents.s: Title cut (when horizontal scroll is forbidden)

documents.t: Each column level that has sub-columns can display a sub-total column summing them (e.g. a Total Country column in a Country > Brand hierarchy). In SDM Xtended Table this is the Show sub-total column field of the column level — On by default at every level — instead of CrossTable's two fixed Show Level 1/2 Sub-Total switches. It has no effect on the last (deepest) column level, which has no sub-columns. A table with four column levels therefore shows sub-totals at levels 1, 2 and 3 by default; uncheck the ones you don't want. Header, data cells and total rows stay aligned: switching a sub-total off removes it everywhere. The Sub-total colors / font / size / bold / italic / underline fields style that sub-total column (header and cells); Inherit from theme keeps the theme's sub-total look. The field stays available even when the level's header is hidden with Show this header: you can hide a level's label and still keep its sub-total. See Totals for how total and sub-total values are computed.

The Column separator field draws a vertical line on the left of each group of the level — useful to visually delimit the countries of a Country > Brand hierarchy, for example without resorting to gaps. Pick a style (Dotted, Dashed, Axis, Solid, Double), then a Separator color and a Separator width (px). None (default) draws nothing. If the level also has a gap, the line is centered in the gap.

The Sample across items field tells the statistics engine how the items of a level relate to each other: Value Meaning Typical use Disjoint (bases add up) (default) Two items are two separate populations: bases add up in totals and in the "complement" of a significance test. Countries, age groups, waves, segments. Shared (same sample, bases don't add up) Items are measured on the same respondents (a battery of items, brands rated by the same people…): a total's base is the base of one item, its value is the average count, and the complement of a significance test isn't inflated by summing the bases. A brand-image grid where all brands were rated by the same 2,500 people. Native (sub-total read from the measure) (columns only) Like Shared, but the sub-total / grand-total value, base and unweighted base are read from the measure itself (Power BI's native sub-total) instead of being recombined from the items. If the measure returns no value (BLANK) for a total, that total falls back to the sum of the items. A DAX measure that already computes the right total (e.g. a deduplicated respondent count). The field is set on the level of the items (e.g. on the Brand level, to say that brands share the same sample, which governs the Year sub-total). On rows, only the last level (the leaf rows) is used; the outer row levels split the table into independent sub-tables and are not affected. Native is a column-only mode — on rows it behaves like Disjoint. This field replaces CrossTable's Multiple answer and Rows are repeated items settings, which do not exist in SDM Xtended Table. See Understanding Bases for the underlying principles and Significance for the effect on tests.

A free-text field, per level, for anything the structured fields above can't express — vertical writing, gradients, custom border styles, letter spacing, whatever your design needs. It's appended, verbatim, to the end of that level's generated CSS rule — after the structured properties, so add !important if you need to override one of them (e.g. background: linear-gradient(...) !important;). border: 2px dashed #999999 !important; border-radius: 6px; 📸 Screenshot — rendered result tableheaders-additionalcss-example.png — a header level styled with the CSS above: a dashed border framing that level's cells. No remote resources Any url(...) fragment is silently stripped before use — the same "no external network access" policy applied to logo images extends to this free-form field, so it can't be used to load a remote background image or font.

A level I added a logo to lost its theme background/text color → set that level's Header colors to Inherit from theme instead of Custom — Custom with empty Background/Font color fields defaults to white/black, overriding the theme. The corner cell (top-left) doesn't match Column Level 1's custom color → Column Level 1's Custom background/font applies to the corner cell too; confirm the report is on a recent version. Logo doesn't show for one header, but shows for others → check both sources: does Header logos have an entry whose label matches that header's exact displayed text, and/or does the Logo series measure return a non-blank value for that header member? Table got slow / truncated after adding a logo → if you're using Logo series, switch to Header logos (the lookup editor) — see the cost explanation above. Additional CSS doesn't seem to apply → structured fields (Background, Font color…) are written with !important; add !important to your own declaration if it's meant to override one of them. Row layout: Hierarchical has no effect → it applies to the outer row levels only (not the last level), and it's ignored in side-by-side (Table of Tables) mode. I don't see an on/off switch to hide a header level → there isn't a separate one; open the relevant ⚙ editor, Add level for that level if it doesn't have a block yet, and uncheck Show this header — see Hiding a header level. Long column titles are cut / my table no longer scrolls horizontally → Forbid horizontal scroll is on; switch it off, or choose another Title cut per level. I can't find Row height, Row group spacing or the Tile mode gaps → they moved into the editors: see Size and Gaps between groups. A sub-total column appeared that I didn't ask for → Show sub-total column is On by default at every column level; uncheck it on the levels where you don't want one.

In survey research, a figure computed on too few respondents is not reliable — and sometimes must not be shown at all (confidentiality, client rules, statistical honesty). The Threshold card automates this with two levels of protection: Warning — the value is displayed, but flagged with a ⚠️ symbol: "interpret with caution".
